### Description

## Description

I am trying to evaluate `lerobot/pi05_libero_finetuned` on LIBERO-10 using the official `lerobot-eval` pipeline. However, the policy gets 0% success and the rollout videos show unintelligent / biased behavior.

This does not seem to be caused by my custom rollout code, because I reproduced the issue using the official `lerobot-eval` command directly.

I also tested `lerobot/pi0_libero_finetuned` in the same environment, and it behaves much more reasonably. In my run, the robot was able to perform meaningful task-directed behavior and picked up the tomato sauce in one episode. This suggests that my LIBERO installation, MuJoCo/EGL rendering, LeRobot environment wrapper, and action interface are working, and the issue may be specific to the `pi05_libero_finetuned` checkpoint or its loading/preprocessing compatibility.

## Command I ran

```bash
cd ~/projects/lerobot

MUJOCO_GL=egl CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 lerobot-eval \
  --policy.path=lerobot/pi05_libero_finetuned \
  --env.type=libero \
  --env.task=libero_10 \
  --env.task_ids='[0]' \
  --eval.batch_size=1 \

2. Run the official `lerobot-eval` command on LIBERO-10 task 0 with `lerobot/pi05_libero_finetuned`.
3. Watch the generated rollout videos and check the final success metric.

## Command I ran

```bash

MUJOCO_GL=egl CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 lerobot-eval \
  --policy.path=lerobot/pi05_libero_finetuned \

Result

The final evaluation reports 0% success:

```Shell
There is no crash. The evaluation runs successfully, but the final success rate is 0%.

Relevant final result:

```

### Checklist

- [ ] I have searched existing tickets to ensure this isn't a duplicate.
- [x] I am using the latest version of the `main` branch.
- [x] I have verified this is not an environment-specific problem.

### Additional Info / Workarounds

## Additional information

I tested `lerobot/pi0_libero_finetuned` in the same environment, and it behaves much more reasonably. In my run, the robot performed meaningful task-directed behavior and picked up the tomato sauce in one episode.

This suggests that the LIBERO installation, MuJoCo/EGL rendering, LeRobot environment wrapper, and action interface are likely working.

## Additional observation from saved rollout videos

I compared the generated videos for three checkpoints in the same LIBERO setup:

- `lerobot/pi05_libero_finetuned`
- `lerobot/pi05_libero_base`
- `lerobot/pi0_libero_finetuned`

In contrast, `lerobot/pi0_libero_finetuned` behaves much more rationally in the same environment. The robot shows task-directed behavior and performs meaningful subtasks. For example, in one episode it picked up the tomato sauce.

- checkpoint conversion issue
- normalization/statistics mismatch
- processor compatibility issue
- expected LeRobot version / commit mismatch

body:
Hi team,

I'm running into a weird issue that's been blocking me for a while. When I train policies (ACT, Pi0, SmolVLA) with a validation split, the robot completely freezes during inference - it just doesn't move at all. But when I train on the full dataset without validation, everything works perfectly.

## The Problem
I have 301 episodes of teleoperation data (15 seconds each) for a weed-pulling task. Here's what happens:
Scenario 1 - With validation (BROKEN):
- Split data: 85% training (256 episodes) + 15% validation (45 episodes)
- Training runs fine, validation loss looks reasonable on WandB
- But at inference: robot doesn't move, actions seem to be near zero
Scenario 2 - Without validation (WORKS):
- Use all 301 episodes for training
- Same hyperparameters, same everything
- Robot works perfectly at inference
I've tested this on ACT, Pi0, and SmolVLA - same issue every time.

## What I think is happening
I suspect there's a normalization statistics mismatch. When you specify `val_episodes`, the dataset still loads the normalization stats from `info.json` which were computed on all 301 episodes. But the training loop only sees 256 episodes, and validation sees 45 different episodes. This creates an inconsistency that breaks action prediction during inference.
Previously I trained on 250 episodes without validation and it worked great, so it's definitely something related to the validation split mechanism.

## Why this matters
I’m analyzing different VLA architectures, and I’d like to know if there are any limitations regarding the validation loss at this stage. Right now I'm stuck either:
- Using validation and getting broken models
- Not using validation and having no proper evaluation methodology
I had to override some code in [lerobot_train.py](lerobot/src/lerobot/scripts/lerobot_train.py)  to add validation support (around lines 396-406) since it wasn't fully implemented, so maybe I'm doing something wrong? Or is this a known limitation?
Would really appreciate any guidance here. Is validation officially supported? If not, what's the recommended way to evaluate models during training?

Thanks!

comments.author: Saad-Mallebhari
comments.body:
@kagyvro48 
I’ve been seeing the same behavior and wanted to share some observations.

When using `val_episodes`, training and validation run normally, but at inference time the policy outputs collapse (near-zero actions). If I train on the full dataset without a validation split, inference works as expected. I’ve observed this consistently across ACT, Pi0, and SmolVLA.

From what I can tell, this seems related to normalization. The stats in `info.json` are computed over the full dataset, while training only sees the training subset when validation is enabled. That mismatch likely causes the policy to operate in a different scale at inference time.

One side effect of this is that actions which are “reasonable” in the model’s normalized space may get scaled down to values that fall below the robot’s effective actuation threshold (deadband), which would explain the frozen behavior despite non-zero predictions.

Another thing worth checking: since validation requires some manual plumbing right now, it’s possible that the training loop or overrides (e.g. in `lerobot_train.py`) are inadvertently mixing normalization stats or switching the model into a state that affects scaling (e.g. BatchNorm / running stats, if present).

If validation is meant to be supported, it seems like normalization should be recomputed strictly from the training split and then reused consistently for training, validation, and inference. As a quick sanity check, one way to confirm this would be:
- recompute normalization using only the training episodes
- save those stats separately
- run inference using that version

If the policy behaves correctly in that setup, it would strongly suggest the issue is due to global normalization rather than model behavior.
Is validation currently expected to work in this configuration, or is the recommended workflow still to train on the full dataset and evaluate separately? Happy to provide a minimal repro or help test a fix if useful.

body:
## Environment & System Info

```shell
- LeRobot version: 0.4.5
- Platform: Linux-6.8.0-101-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.35
- Python version: 3.10.19
- Huggingface Hub version: 1.5.0
- Datasets version: 4.6.1
- Numpy version: 2.2.6
- FFmpeg version: 4.4.2-0ubuntu0.22.04.1
- PyTorch version: 2.5.1+cu121
- Is PyTorch built with CUDA support?: True
- Cuda version: 12.1
- GPU model: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Laptop GPU
- Using GPU in script?: Yes
```

## Description

I hit a reproducible low-VRAM failure mode when evaluating `lerobot/smolvla_base` on LIBERO using an `8GB` GPU.

The default evaluation flow loads:

1. the SmolVLA policy on CUDA, and
2. the MuJoCo/robosuite environment with EGL rendering

inside the same OS process.

On my setup, this causes the evaluation to fail during environment initialization because the PyTorch CUDA context and the EGL rendering context compete for limited GPU memory.

As a workaround, I implemented a local 2-process evaluation path:

- **Process A**: loads the SmolVLA model on GPU and runs inference
- **Process B**: owns the LIBERO environment and EGL rendering

The two processes communicate over subprocess `stdin/stdout` using:

- JSON headers for metadata
- binary NumPy payloads for large arrays

This avoids the CUDA/EGL collision and makes evaluation feasible on an `8GB` GPU. For IPC, large arrays need binary transfer; naive array serialization was too slow in local testing.

I wanted to check whether maintainers would be interested in an upstream contribution for this as either:

- a low-VRAM eval example for `smolvla + libero`
- a dedicated utility/script for process-isolated evaluation
- or a smaller integration into the existing evaluation flow

## Context & Reproduction

### Hardware

- RTX 3070 Laptop GPU (`8GB`)

### Failure mode

- evaluate `lerobot/smolvla_base` on LIBERO
- MuJoCo uses EGL
- single-process evaluation fails on a small GPU because the model and renderer share the same process/GPU memory budget

In my setup, this usually manifests as abrupt process termination / OOM-style failure rather than a stable Python traceback.

### Local workaround

I built a 2-process evaluator with these files:

- `eval_8gb/eval_libero_8gb.py`
- `eval_8gb/env_worker.py`

High-level flow:

1. main process loads the policy on CUDA
2. subprocess creates the LIBERO env and renders observations
3. observations are sent to the model process
4. actions are returned to the env worker

Additional fixes required during implementation:

- using `obs_type="pixels_agent_pos"` so LIBERO returns robot state
- camera name remapping for SmolVLA-compatible keys
- redirecting worker `stdout` to `stderr` so library prints do not corrupt the IPC stream

## Local outcome

On my setup:

- the default single-process path fails during evaluation setup on an `8GB` GPU
- the 2-process path runs successfully

One prototype measurement I recorded locally was that a `1000`-step run dropped from `>2.5 hours` with naive array serialization to about `32 seconds` once large arrays were transferred as binary payloads.

I would still treat that runtime number as preliminary until I rerun it in a cleaned version.

## Example command

```bash
export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/LIBERO:$PYTHONPATH
python eval_8gb/eval_libero_8gb.py \
  --policy_path lerobot/smolvla_base \
  --task libero_10 \
  --n_episodes 5
```

## Question

Would maintainers be interested in a cleaned PR for this?

If yes, I can reduce the current prototype to a narrow contribution with:

- minimal scope
- docs
- focused tests for the IPC helpers
- explicit AI-assistance disclosure in the PR description

comments.author: Lidang-Jiang
comments.body:
Hi @proxi666, thanks for the detailed issue and the working prototype design!

I've submitted a PR #3235 that integrates process-isolated evaluation into the existing eval pipeline as a new `--eval.process_isolated=true` flag.

**Key design:**
- Single subprocess manages all environments with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""` + `MUJOCO_GL=osmesa`
- `EnvProxy` implements the `VectorEnv` interface subset used by `rollout()`, so the existing eval code works unchanged
- Thread-safe IPC via `multiprocessing.Pipe` with a shared lock
- Cached task descriptions and episode steps to minimize IPC overhead
- `atexit` cleanup and 120s startup timeout for robustness

The implementation was inspired by your 2-process design (JSON headers + binary NumPy payloads). The upstream version uses `multiprocessing.Pipe` (pickle-based) which handles numpy array serialization efficiently out of the box.

Would love your feedback on the approach!

comments.author: rylinjames
comments.body: the cuda-context vs egl contention on 8gb is a real pain, your 2-process split is the right shape. one thing worth checking: if you pass `MUJOCO_GL=osmesa` or `glfw` headless instead of egl, the gpu-memory competition goes away entirely at the cost of cpu rendering (slower but feasible for eval). that's a simpler upstream story than a full ipc harness. for the ipc path, if you end up shipping it, using posix shared-memory (via multiprocessing.shared_memory) for the image tensors avoids the stdin/stdout serialization overhead entirely. reflex-vla (open-source deploy layer for smolvla/pi0/pi0.5/gr00t) runs policy server in a separate process by default on jetson exactly to avoid this class of bug, similar split to what you built. github.com/rylinjames/reflex-vla. good-first-issues tagged there if you want to poke around, or dm romirj on discord / playindus@gmail.com for collaborator access.

body:
Hi LeRobot team,

First of all, thank you for the amazing work on SmolVLA and the LeRobot library!

I am currently trying to reproduce the SmolVLA results on the LIBERO benchmark. To make the comparison as fair as possible, I aligned my setup with the details described in the paper:

* **Section 4.7 (Ablation):** no robotics pretraining, frozen VLM backbone, and only the action expert trained from scratch (`load_vlm_weights=True`, `freeze_vision_encoder=True`, `train_expert_only=True`)
* **Section 4.3 (Implementation details):** 100,000 training steps with batch size 64 for simulation benchmarks

With that setup, I do get a working policy and reasonable learning behavior, but my results are still noticeably below the paper on several LIBERO suites.

**My evaluation results (batch size 64, 100k steps, 10 episodes per task):**

* **libero_10 (Long):** 44.8% (paper: ~71%)
* **libero_spatial:** 83.0% (paper: ~90%)
* **libero_object:** 70.0% (paper: ~96%)
* **libero_goal:** 70.0% (paper: ~92%)

So I wanted to ask whether I may still be missing an important detail in the intended reproduction recipe.

In particular, could you clarify:

1. **Are the high LIBERO numbers in the main table directly comparable to the “frozen VLM + expert-only from scratch” setup described in the ablation section, or was a meaningfully different training recipe used for the main reported numbers?**

2. For the LIBERO results in the paper, was the model trained as:

   * **one single multi-task policy over all 40 tasks**, or
   * **separate policies per suite / subset**?

   I am currently training a single multi-task model across all 40 tasks, so I wanted to confirm whether that matches the paper setup.

3. Could you share the exact reproduction details for the LIBERO experiments, if possible?

   * exact `lerobot-train` command or `.yaml` config
   * learning rate and scheduler
   * global/effective batch size and GPU count
   * evaluation details for LIBERO
   * specific commit hash used for the paper experiments

At this point I can reproduce a functional policy, but I am still significantly below the paper on several suites, so I would really appreciate any clarification on the exact recipe.

Thank you in advance for your time and guidance!

comments.author: CarolinePascal
comments.body:
Hi @SlenderMongoose,

Thank you for reporting on the v0.5.0 right after the release ! Regarding your observations on Libero with pi0.5, this is indeed a side effect of the latest release. 
In v0.5.0, we had to fix two issues :
- Removing the padding of images stored as `float32` in [0,1] before applying the signup norm;
- Removing the padding of the state in the pi0.5 processor.

As a consequence, the checkpoints and fine-tuned weights obtained in v.04.4 will no longer work as expected in v.0.5.0. New checkpoints are available here : https://huggingface.co/lerobot/pi05-libero and legacy checkpoints are still available here : https://huggingface.co/lerobot/pi0fast-libero-v044. You will likely need to fine-tune again to reach the same performances.

Regarding Gr00t, I'll have a look at our implementation asap !

Best,

Caroline

body:
### Ticket Type

🐛 Bug Report (Something isn't working)

### Environment & System Info

```Shell

```

### Description

When running the evaluation pipeline with a model that utilizes `bfloat16` (e.g. for `flash-attn`), the pipeline crashes during the conversion of actions to Numpy arrays.

The issue stems from the `DeviceProcessorStep` in the environment post-processor. While it correctly moves the tensor to the CPU, it does not cast it to `float32` because the default configuration on `lerobot/xvla-libero` initializes `float_dtype` as `null`. Since Numpy does not natively support `bfloat16` for many standard operations/conversions on all systems, calling `.numpy()` on the CPU tensor results in a `TypeError`.

### **Reproduction Context**
1. Train or load a policy that outputs tensors in `torch.bfloat16`.
2. Run the standard `lerobot` evaluation pipeline.
3. The crash occurs in the evaluation loop at the point of Numpy conversion.

**Relevant Code Snippet (Evaluation Loop):**
```python
observation = preprocessor(observation)
with torch.inference_mode():
    action = policy.select_action(observation) # Returns bfloat16
action = postprocessor(action) # Moves to CPU, but keeps bfloat16

action_transition = {ACTION: action}
action_transition = env_postprocessor(action_transition) 
action = action_transition[ACTION]

# CRASH HAPPENS HERE
action_numpy: np.ndarray = action.to("cpu").numpy()
assert action_numpy.ndim == 2, "Action dimensions should be (batch, action_dim)"
```

### **Root Cause Analysis**

The env_postprocessor utilizes DeviceProcessorStep. In the current configuration, it is initialized as follows:

```json
{
  "registry_name": "device_processor",
  "config": {
    "device": "cpu",
    "float_dtype": null
  }
}
```
Because float_dtype is `null`, the processor moves the data to the CPU but preserves the `bfloat16` data type. When the pipeline attempts to convert this to a Numpy array via `.numpy()`, it fails because Numpy cannot handle the `bfloat16` format in this context.


### **Expected Behavior**

The evaluation pipeline should automatically handle bfloat16 model outputs. When the DeviceProcessorStep moves tensors to the CPU for environment interaction, it should ensure the dtype is cast to `float32` to maintain compatibility with Numpy and the Gym/Gymnasium interface.

### **Proposed Solution**

The device_processor configuration in config.json should be updated to default float_dtype to float32 instead of null.

Suggested Config Change:
```json
"registry_name": "device_processor",
"config": {
  "device": "cpu",
  "float_dtype": "float32"
}
```` 

### Context & Reproduction

_No response_

### Relevant logs or stack trace

```Shell

```

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing tickets to ensure this isn't a duplicate.
- [x] I am using the latest version of the `main` branch.
- [x] I have verified this is not an environment-specific problem.

### Additional Info / Workarounds

I have developed a monkey patch to force float32 casting in the DeviceProcessorStep, which resolves the issue:

```python
def force_device_processor_float32():
    """
    Explicitly casts predicted actions from bfloat16 to float32 to ensure 
    compatibility with numpy in the eval pipeline.
    """
    from lerobot.common.datasets.utils import DeviceProcessorStep 

    original_init = DeviceProcessorStep.__init__

    def forced_init(self, *args, **kwargs):
        # Force float32 if no dtype is specified
        if kwargs.get("float_dtype") is None:
            kwargs["float_dtype"] = "float32"
        original_init(self, *args, **kwargs)

    # Apply the monkey patch
    DeviceProcessorStep.__init__ = forced_init
```

Oh no, in the pretrained lerobot/xvla-folding checkpoint, the model was trained with max_len_seq = 512, so the positional embedding table is only initialized up to length 512.
Simply setting policy.max_len_seq = <larger> at inference time does not automatically resize or reinitialize the positional embeddings. So i would suggest fine tuninng with. a max_len of 1254 if that's what you want. Lmk how it goes!

Hey, if anybody else comes across this issue, I had something similar happen to me. The issue was that my `tokenizer_max_length` in the `TokenizerProcessorStep` of the preprocessing pipeline was not set to the correct value of 50 but a much higher value, resulting in a large amount of text tokens and a overly long total input sequence.
Ensuring that the max_lenght is 50 solved the issue for me.

body:
Hi, everyone!

Seems like the pi0.5 evaluation on libero differs from the setup used in the original openpi implementation:
- the command from the [documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/libero#reproducing-%CF%80%E2%82%80%E2%82%85-results) uses `--eval.batch_size=1` and `--eval.n_episodes=10`. Thus, for each task group and task, only one enviroment will be created with a fixed initial_state: `episode_idx = 0` [here](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/src/lerobot/envs/libero.py#L312). While there are 10 episodes in the evaluation for each task, each rollout will just reset the environment and start from the same initial state, because `env.num_envs` is 1 [here](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/src/lerobot/scripts/lerobot_eval.py#L277)
- in the original openpi evaluation script, each episode sets its own initial state for each task [code](https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi/blob/main/examples/libero/main.py#L97)

So, the the command from the docs evaulates the policy using the same initial configuration of the environment 10 times, while the original openpi repo evaluates on 10 different initial configurations.

However, I couldn't figure out how to fix it quickly because I would like to use similar logic from the eval script to record rollouts of the policy to generate some data and I need to set different initial configurations for each rollout. Seems like the eval script [has](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/src/lerobot/scripts/lerobot_eval.py#L584) the implementation of this logic on some level but never saves the trajectories.

For your case, the evaluation error occurs because the `smolvla_base` model was trained for a 6-dimensional action space (SO-101 arm), but you are using it in the Libero environment, which requires a 7-dimensional action space (Franka arm). This mismatch will always trigger an assertion error.

body:
Hi,

There is a video decoder benchmark that lerobot uses that evaluates video decoders for accuracy and performance, example this:

```
python run_video_benchmark.py     --output-dir outputs/video_benchmark     --repo-ids         lerobot/pusht_image         aliberts/aloha_mobile_shrimp_image     --vcodec libsvtav1     --pix-fmt yuv444p yuv420p     --g 2 20 None     --crf 10 40 None     --timestamps-modes 1_frame 2_frames     --backends pyav      --num-samples 5     --num-workers 5     --save-frames 1
```

The benchmark requests frames at certain timestamps in the video, and then gets back decoded frames and timestamps that the decoder sends. Correct me if I am wrong but the benchmark then looks at the distance between the query timestamp and the decoded timestamp to see how accurate the decoder was.

https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/8c4643687c97ffafeecd78a7cde5504febe3427e/lerobot/common/datasets/video_utils.py#L132-L162

This is well-intentioned, but there is a technical point here -- frames of a video are not instants in point of time -- they are interval (typically have a presentation timestamp and a duration).

Imagine the scenario in this diagram:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2a1b6f6e-398a-4209-a5ea-ff960097dcda)

The query timestamp is 0.99. Imagine two decoders -- one returns frame0 with pts=0 and another returns frame1 with pts=1.

The current code will look at the distance of the pts with the query timestamp and think frame1 is more "accurate".

However, at timestamp=0.99, frame0 is the one that's actually displayed! So clearly frame0 is the more accurate choice even though the distance metric judges it to be less accurate.

I propose a couple of solutions here:

1. Have decoders return an interval for the frame instead of a single point in time, and then the code that does the accuracy evaluation should look for the nearest point in the frame to the query timestamp.
2. Have the decoders or wrappers themselves return the closest point within the frame interval to the query timestamp. But this involves changing the API of the decoder.

I actually think decoders going forward should standardize their API on (1) -- i.e. when they return the frame they should return the *interval*, not just a single point in time, to represent the interval of time the frame is visible.

TorchCodec, already returns an interval (https://github.com/pytorch/torchcodec/blob/f4065f1b477148cfb0ef94167fb0bf3a63803e55/src/torchcodec/decoders/_simple_video_decoder.py#L39-L42) but some other decoders just return a single point in time.

comments.author: aliberts
comments.body:
Hello there,
Thank you for the time you put into this, that's an interesting insight!

Our video benchmark evaluates 3 things:
- Video encoding/decoding quality (through several metrics)
- The size of encoded video vs the size of its set of unencoded frames
- The time it takes for decoding frames vs the time it takes to read those frames from image files

Accuracy is not evaluated. We do that have that tolerance check in the decoding function to make sure we don't accidentally retrieve a frame that's too far off the requested timestamp (which could reveal a config issue, e.g. like wrong fps) but it's not a metric. Moreover, for the purpose of this benchmark, the only thing that matters is when sampling a timestamp we get the same frame associated to that timestamp whether its from the video or the images (which it is).

Now more generally within our datasets, we typically have visual modality (videos) and the robot's proprioception (states/actions as vectors) which are recorded in sync under the same timestamp. During inference, we fetch the most recent "picture" (frame and state) of the robot in order to have the most up-to-date information to do inference with and so the "requested timestamp" will always be at the start of the frame. This is why we're mostly interested in the frame that starts the closest to the requested timestamp. Does that make sense?

cc @Cadene

### Reproduction

When I run the following command on M3 Mac

```
python lerobot/scripts/train.py \
    device=mps \
    env=aloha \
    policy=act 
```

Evaluation will sometimes fail with this error:
```
dm_control.rl.control.PhysicsError: Physics state is invalid. Warning(s) raised: mjWARN_BADCTRL
```

This error is caused by NaN values outputted by the policy being inputted Mujoco Env. 

The issue seems to be caused here:
https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/77478d50e5d5642112d1bad6f1657f08eb1c3378/lerobot/scripts/eval.py#L152

For some reason when using GPU on my Mac this line causes issues and will cause observation to have abnormal values.

For example if I add the following code below this line:
```
# check for any val greater in mag than 10
if torch.any(observation["observation.state"] > 10):
    print(f"Value greater than 10 found, {torch.max(observation['observation.state'])}")
```

I'll get this output
```
Value greater than 10 found, 18352227483648.0
|█████████████▍                                                   | 83/400 [00:01<00:06, 46.59it/s, running_success_rate=0.0%]
Value greater than 10 found, 8214175285248.0%
|█████████████▉                                                   | 86/400 [00:01<00:06, 46.57it/s, running_success_rate=0.0%]
Value greater than 10 found, 18776087068672.0
```

Which doesn't make sense for the gym_aloha env state observations.

I fixed this issue by not overwriting observation and instead making a new variable:
```
new_observation = {key: observation[key].to(device, non_blocking=True) for key in observation}

with torch.inference_mode():
    action = policy.select_action(new_observation)
```

### Expected behavior

Eval should run smoothly without raising error

comments.author: alexander-soare
comments.body:
@Jubayer-Hamid thanks for raising this. VQ-BeT and Diffusion Policy should give about the same results. In fact, the models we have on the hub ([DP](https://huggingface.co/lerobot/diffusion_pusht), [VQ-BeT](https://huggingface.co/lerobot/vqbet_pusht)) happen to both give 63.8% success rate with 500 evals.

If you try running evals with:
`python lerobot/eval/scripts.py -p path/to/pretrained_model eval.n_episodes=500 eval.batch_size=50 eval.use_async_envs=true use_amp=true`, what do you get?
The curves your are showing are likely only using 50 evaluation episodes if you used default settings, meaning the variance is quite high.

body:
Hello,

Lerobot has officially ported [LIBERO](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/issues/1369#issuecomment-3323183721), and we can use the checkpoint at [HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero) to evaluate the LIBERO benchmark.

However, the model configuration of [HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero) appears to differ from the [original model](https://huggingface.co/lerobot/smolvla_base). For example:

[lerobot/smolvla_base](https://huggingface.co/lerobot/smolvla_base/blob/main/config.json)
```json
{
  "vlm_model_name": "HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-500M-Video-Instruct",
  "load_vlm_weights": true,
  "add_image_special_tokens": false,
  "attention_mode": "cross_attn",
  "prefix_length": 0,
  "pad_language_to": "max_length",
  "num_expert_layers": 0,
  "num_vlm_layers": 16,
  "self_attn_every_n_layers": 2,
  "expert_width_multiplier": 0.75
}
```

[HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceVLA/smolvla_libero/blob/main/config.json)
```json
{
  "vlm_model_name": "HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-500M-Instruct",
  "load_vlm_weights": true,
  "add_image_special_tokens": false,
  "attention_mode": "cross_attn",
  "prefix_length": 0,
  "pad_language_to": "longest",
  "num_expert_layers": -1,
  "num_vlm_layers": 0, <- it becomes 32  when model is initialized
  "self_attn_every_n_layers": 2,
  "expert_width_multiplier": 0.5,
}
```

In particular, `num_vlm_layers` is set to 32 across all layers, which is not consistent with the [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.01844) where they use half of them (16 layers).
Could you provide the original model checkpoint and the training recipe so we can reproduce the LIBERO benchmark performance?

comments.author: mokpo4550
comments.body:
I am currently using `lerobot` version 0.4.4. 

To train a GROOT model, I recorded and merged multiple datasets: several object-specific lifting datasets and a "wait" task dataset where the robot just stays at its initial position regardless of the object. 

During inference, however, the model ignored the given task commands, leading to a significant drop in success rate.

The issue stems from "processor_groot.py". When processing a data batch, the task instruction for the entire batch is overwritten by the first task instruction: `lang = lang[0] if len(lang) > 0 else "Perform the task."`

This causes all items in the batch to share the exact same task instruction, overriding individual tasks.

**How I Fixed This**
I resolved this by updating processor_groot.py so that each batch index handles its own corresponding task. I also fixed a formatting bug where the entire list (including brackets [...]) was incorrectly stringified into text_content.

#### 1. `GrootPackInputsStep.__call__` (around Line 289)
**Before:**
```python
if isinstance(lang, list):
    lang = lang[0] if len(lang) > 0 else None

```

**After:**

```python
# Commented out to prevent flattening the list prematurely
# if isinstance(lang, list):
#     lang = lang[0] if len(lang) > 0 else None

```

#### 2. `GrootEagleEncodeStep.__call__` (around Line 453)

**Before:**

```python
lang = comp.get("language", "Perform the task.")
if isinstance(lang, list):
    lang = lang[0] if len(lang) > 0 else "Perform the task."

```

**After:**

```python
lang = comp.get("language", ["Perform the task."])
if not isinstance(lang, list):
    lang = [lang]

```

#### 3. `GrootEagleEncodeStep.__call__` (around Line 470)

**Before:**

```python
lang_formatted = str([lang])

```

**After:**

```python
lang_formatted = str(lang[b])

```

Hi,
I’m running ACT training on my custom SO-101 robot setup (based on so101_follower + so101_leader teleop).
After training ~100k steps, my robot’s learned policy shows almost no meaningful motion — it doesn’t approach or grasp the object, even though the dataset and training logs look fine.

I suspect this might be related to training stability (batch size, accumulation, or gradient scaling), but I’d like your advice on how to debug this properly.


lerobot-train \
  --dataset.repo_id=${HF_USER}/record-test \
  --policy.type=act \
  --output_dir=ooutputs/train/act_so101_1 \
  --job_name=act_so101_test \
  --policy.device=cuda \
  --wandb.enable=false \
  --policy.repo_id=${HF_USER}/my_act_policy-v1 \
  --steps 100000 \
  --batch_size 1 \
  --policy.chunk_size=50 \
  --policy.n_action_steps=50 \
  --policy.n_encoder_layers=2 \
  --policy.use_vae=false \
  --policy.use_amp=true \
  --log_freq 50 \
  --eval_freq 100


Hardware:

GPU: RTX 3060 (8 GB VRAM)

OS: Ubuntu 22.04 / CUDA 12.4

Dataset: 49 episodes (~39k frames, two 1080p camera views)

Policy params: ~26 M (ResNet18 backbone, Transformer encoder-decoder)

Expected behavior

After ~30k–100k steps, the ACT policy should at least learn smooth approach or grasp-like motion in replay or real execution.

Actual behavior

Training completes without crash, loss decreases slowly.
During replay (via robot_client.py), robot stays static or moves unpredictably.
Increasing steps doesn’t help much — probably due to very small batch (batch = 1).

Attempted fixes

Enabled --policy.gradient_checkpointing=true
Tried --policy.use_amp=true
Modified training script to simulate gradient accumulation (accum_steps = 16)
Verified dataset integrity (39k frames, correct camera pairs, proper calibration)
Still, the learned policy produces weak or unstable control outputs.

Questions
Does ACT require a minimum batch size (e.g. ≥ 16) for stable gradient updates?
Is there a recommended gradient accumulation approach compatible with lerobot-train?
Could I safely downscale camera images (1080p → 480p) to allow larger batches without hurting performance?
Are there best practices for balancing chunk_size and n_action_steps for small datasets?

comments.author: Rahillasne
comments.body:
Batch size 1 is your main problem — ACT needs at least 8 for stable gradients. Downscale your cameras to 480×480 (original ACT used this, no quality loss for tabletop tasks) and you should fit batch=16 on a 3060.
Also: chunk_size=50 and n_action_steps=50 is way too high. Try chunk_size=20, n_action_steps=10. And turn use_vae=true back on — without it, ACT averages contradictory demonstrations into mush.
I ran your dataset format through a quality checker I built (pip install orbit-robotics) — for SO-101 setups with 49 episodes it'll tell you if you have dead joints, action divergence, or consistency issues that explain the failure before you burn more GPU hours. Might save you some debugging time.

comments.author: jashshah999
comments.body:
A common cause of "robot not moving" is idle/static frames dominating the dataset, biasing the policy toward zero-action predictions. `lerobot-doctor trim` detects and removes these static frames automatically. Also `lerobot-doctor score` identifies low-quality episodes that might be poisoning training.

```bash
lerobot-doctor trim /path/to/dataset --dry-run
lerobot-doctor score /path/to/dataset
```

https://github.com/jashshah999/lerobot-doctor

comments.author: Lynn-hh
comments.body:
I looked into this and have a minimal, hardware-free reproduction. The root
cause is that the async policy server serves observations one at a time and
calls `predict_action_chunk` directly, but Diffusion Policy requires
`n_obs_steps` (default 2) stacked observations. ACT works because its
`n_obs_steps == 1`.

Minimal repro (no robot/GPU needed):

```python
import torch
from lerobot.policies.diffusion.configuration_diffusion import DiffusionConfig
from lerobot.policies.diffusion.modeling_diffusion import DiffusionPolicy
from lerobot.configs.types import PolicyFeature, FeatureType

cfg = DiffusionConfig(
    n_obs_steps=2, horizon=16, n_action_steps=8, crop_shape=None,
    input_features={
        "observation.image": PolicyFeature(type=FeatureType.VISUAL, shape=(3, 96, 96)),
        "observation.state": PolicyFeature(type=FeatureType.STATE, shape=(4,)),
    },
    output_features={"action": PolicyFeature(type=FeatureType.ACTION, shape=(4,))},
)
stats = {k: {"mean": torch.zeros(s), "std": torch.ones(s), "min": torch.zeros(s), "max": torch.ones(s)}
         for k, s in {"observation.image": (3,1,1), "observation.state": (4,), "action": (4,)}.items()}
policy = DiffusionPolicy(cfg, dataset_stats=stats).eval()
policy.reset()
# Async server feeds a single live frame and calls predict_action_chunk directly:
policy.predict_action_chunk({
    "observation.image": torch.randn(1, 3, 96, 96),
    "observation.state": torch.randn(1, 4),
})
# -> AssertionError at modeling_diffusion.py generate_actions:
#    assert n_obs_steps == self.config.n_obs_steps
```

In the full async path this surfaces as the reporter's "stack expects a
non-empty TensorList", but the underlying cause is the same: `n_obs_steps > 1`
policies aren't given an observation history when served via
`predict_action_chunk`.

I'd be happy to open a PR. Two possible directions — which do you prefer?
1. Have `predict_action_chunk` build/maintain the observation history (mirror
   what `select_action` already does via the queues), so single-frame live
   serving fills `n_obs_steps` (copying the first obs at episode start).
2. Handle the history accumulation on the async `policy_server` side.

I'll include a regression test either way. (Note: AI-assisted investigation.)

## Description
RTC inference calls `policy.predict_action_chunk(batch, inference_delay=..., prev_chunk_left_over=...)`. ACT and Diffusion Policy have strict signatures without `**kwargs`, causing rollout to crash:
```
TypeError: ACTPolicy.predict_action_chunk() got an unexpected keyword argument inference_delay
TypeError: DiffusionPolicy.predict_action_chunk() got an unexpected keyword argument inference_delay

SmolVLA already accepts `**kwargs` and works fine.

## Affected policies
- `src/lerobot/policies/act/modeling_act.py:126`
- `src/lerobot/policies/diffusion/modeling_diffusion.py:103`

## Fix
Add `**kwargs` to both signatures, matching SmolVLA.

### Ticket Type

💡 Feature Request / Improvement

### Environment & System Info

```Shell
- LeRobot version: 0.5.2
- Platform: Linux-6.14.0-1020-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39
- Python version: 3.12.13
- Huggingface Hub version: 1.20.1
- Transformers version: 5.5.4
- Datasets version: 4.8.5
- Numpy version: 2.2.6
- FFmpeg version: 6.1.1-3ubuntu5
- PyTorch version: 2.10.0+cu128
- Torchcodec version: 0.10.0
- Is PyTorch built with CUDA support?: True
- Cuda version: 12.8
- GPU model: NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation
- Using GPU in script?: <fill in>
- lerobot scripts: ['lerobot-annotate', 'lerobot-calibrate', 'lerobot-dataset-viz', 'lerobot-edit-dataset', 'lerobot-eval', 'lerobot-find-cameras', 'lerobot-find-joint-limits', 'lerobot-find-port', 'lerobot-imgtransform-viz', 'lerobot-info', 'lerobot-record', 'lerobot-replay', 'lerobot-rollout', 'lerobot-setup-can', 'lerobot-setup-motors', 'lerobot-teleoperate', 'lerobot-train', 'lerobot-train-tokenizer']
```

### Description

## Summary

`RelativeActionsProcessorStep` (and the underlying `to_relative_actions` /
`to_absolute_actions`) compute the relative-action base as `state[..., :action_dim]`.
This silently assumes that the first `action_dim` channels of `observation.state`
are **positionally aligned** with `action` (i.e. `state[i]` is the quantity that
`action[i]` controls). That assumption only holds when the state is a prefix-aligned
copy of the action, and breaks for almost any realistic observation layout.

## Goal / use case

Make relative actions work correctly when `observation.state` is **not** a prefix
copy of the action. This is the common case in real manipulation:

- **Interleaved `[pos, vel]` per joint** — e.g. state =
  `[j0p, j0v, j1p, j1v, ..., j5p, j5v, grip]` (13) but action =
  `[j0p..j5p, grip]` (7). The relative base must pull the *position* channels
  `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]`, not `state[:7]` (which mixes in velocities and the
  wrong joints).
- **State augmented with force/torque, EE pose, contact flags, or joint currents** —
  any extra proprioceptive channel shifts the alignment and corrupts the base.

When the layout doesn't match the implicit prefix assumption, the wrong state
columns are subtracted (preprocess) and added back (postprocess), so the model
trains on corrupted relative targets and eval produces wrong absolute actions —
**with no error and no warning**.

## Proposed change

Add an optional, explicit/name-based mapping from action dims to state columns,
defaulting to the current `state[:action_dim]` behavior so it is fully backward
compatible:

- `state_action_index_map: list[int] | None` — entry `i` is the `observation.state`
  column that action dim `i` is relative to.
- `state_names` / `state_feature_names` — when given alongside `action_feature_names`
  (and no explicit map), resolve the mapping by matching names.
- A validation guard that raises on length/range mismatch instead of silently
  producing wrong offsets.

Used symmetrically by `RelativeActionsProcessorStep` (preprocess) and
`AbsoluteActionsProcessorStep` (postprocess) so train and eval stay consistent.

## Notes

- Backward compatible: with no map and no names, behavior is identical to today.
- I have a working implementation and can open a PR.

### Context & Reproduction

## Where it happens

`src/lerobot/processor/relative_action_processor.py` — both helpers hardcode the
relative base as the first `action_dim` channels of the state:

```python
def to_relative_actions(actions, state, mask):
    ...
    state_offset = state[..., :dims] * mask_t   # <-- assumes prefix alignment
    actions[..., :dims] -= state_offset
    return actions

def to_absolute_actions(actions, state, mask):
    ...
    state_offset = state[..., :dims] * mask_t   # <-- same assumption on the way back
    actions[..., :dims] += state_offset
    return actions
```

`RelativeActionsProcessorStep.__call__` caches `observation.state` and calls
`to_relative_actions`; `AbsoluteActionsProcessorStep.__call__` reuses the cached
state via `to_absolute_actions`. Neither offers a way to map an action dim to a
non-contiguous / non-prefix state channel, and there is no validation when the
layouts don't line up.

## Minimal reproduction

State is interleaved `[pos, vel]` per joint + gripper (13), action is
`[j0p..j5p, grip]` (7). The correct relative base is the position channels
`[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]`.

```python
import torch
from lerobot.processor.relative_action_processor import (
    to_relative_actions, to_absolute_actions,
)

# state: [j0p, j0v, j1p, j1v, ..., j5p, j5v, grip]  (13)
state  = torch.tensor([[10., 0.1, 20., 0.2, 30., 0.3,
                        40., 0.4, 50., 0.5, 60., 0.6, 99.]])
# action: [j0p..j5p, grip]  (7), absolute joint targets
action = torch.tensor([[11., 22., 33., 44., 55., 66., 7.]])
mask   = [True] * 6 + [False]          # gripper kept absolute

# --- current behaviour: base = state[:7] = [j0p, j0v, j1p, j1v, j2p, j2v, j3p]
rel = to_relative_actions(action, state, mask)
print(rel.tolist())
# [[1.0, 21.9, 13.0, 43.8, 25.0, 65.7, 7.0]]
#        ^^^^        ^^^^        ^^^^  velocities / wrong joints leak into the base
```

Expected (base = position channels `[0,2,4,6,8,10,12]`): clean per-joint offsets
`[[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]]`. Because the base is wrong, the model trains on
corrupted relative targets, and at inference `to_absolute_actions` adds the same
wrong base back — the policy ends up commanding the wrong joint positions (in our
case, consistently missing grasps). **No error or warning is raised.**

## Proposed fix (working locally)

Add an optional `state_index_map` so the base is selected explicitly, defaulting
to the current prefix behaviour:

```python
def _state_base_offset(state, mask_t, state_index_map):
    dims = mask_t.shape[0]
    if state_index_map is not None:
        idx = torch.as_tensor(list(state_index_map), dtype=torch.long, device=state.device)
        base = state.index_select(-1, idx)        # explicit per-action-dim base
    else:
        base = state[..., :dims]                  # legacy prefix (unchanged)
    return base * mask_t
```

Round-trip with the map is exact:

```python
idx_map = [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
rel  = to_relative_actions(action, state, mask, idx_map)   # [[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]]
back = to_absolute_actions(rel, state, mask, idx_map)      # == action
assert torch.allclose(back, action)
```

`RelativeActionsProcessorStep` / `AbsoluteActionsProcessorStep` expose this via:

- `state_action_index_map: list[int] | None` — explicit action→state column map.
- `state_names` + `action_feature_names` — resolve the map by matching names when
  no explicit map is given.
- A guard that raises on length/range mismatch instead of silently mis-aligning.

For pi0 it's surfaced as `PI0Config.relative_state_index_map` (and
`state_feature_names`), threaded through `make_pi0_pre_post_processors`. Fully
backward compatible: with no map and no names, behaviour is identical to today.

### Relevant logs or stack trace

```Shell

```

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing tickets to ensure this isn't a duplicate.
- [x] I am using the latest version of the `main` branch.
- [x] I have verified this is not an environment-specific problem.

### Additional Info / Workarounds

## Production-level fix (proposed for upstream)

Name-based alignment as the default, with an explicit index map as an override.
Because every action dim and every state channel already carry names in the
dataset metadata, the base for action dim `i` should be resolved by **matching
names**, not by position:

- Default: match `action_feature_names[i]` to the identically named
  `observation.state` channel (e.g. action `joint_0.pos` → state `joint_0.pos`).
  Dims with no matching state channel (or listed in `exclude_joints`, like the
  gripper) stay absolute.
- Override: an explicit `state_action_index_map` for layouts where names are
  unavailable or ambiguous.
- Guard: raise on length/range mismatch so misalignment fails loudly instead of
  silently corrupting targets.

This generalizes to any observation layout — interleaved `[pos, vel]`, or state
augmented with force/torque, EE pose, contact flags, joint currents — without
per-dataset hacks. The current `state[:action_dim]` becomes the special case
where names happen to line up by position.

## Local fix / workaround (works today)

If you can't wait for upstream, the minimal change is to make the relative base
selectable and pass the position indices explicitly.

**1. Make the base selectable** (`relative_action_processor.py`):

```python
def _state_base_offset(state, mask_t, state_index_map):
    dims = mask_t.shape[0]
    if state_index_map is not None:
        idx = torch.as_tensor(list(state_index_map), dtype=torch.long, device=state.device)
        base = state.index_select(-1, idx)   # explicit per-action-dim base
    else:
        base = state[..., :dims]             # legacy prefix (unchanged)
    return base * mask_t
```

`to_relative_actions` / `to_absolute_actions` take an optional
`state_index_map`; `RelativeActionsProcessorStep` / `AbsoluteActionsProcessorStep`
hold and forward it (explicit map, or name-resolved from `state_names` +
`action_feature_names`).

**2. Surface it on the policy config** (`PI0Config`):

```python
relative_state_index_map: list[int] | None = None
state_feature_names: list[str] | None = None
```

threaded into `make_pi0_pre_post_processors` → `RelativeActionsProcessorStep`.

**3. Set the map for your dataset.** For an interleaved
`[j0p, j0v, ..., j5p, j5v, grip]` (13) state with `[j0p..j5p, grip]` (7) action:

```yaml
# training config
policy:
  use_relative_actions: true
  relative_exclude_joints: ["gripper"]
  relative_state_index_map: [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]   # position channels only
```

**Workaround without touching the processor** (if you only need it to work, not
to fix the library): re-layout the dataset so the **first `action_dim` state
channels are the absolute action quantities** (e.g. store `observation.state` as
`[j0p..j5p, grip, j0v..j5v, ...]` instead of interleaved). Then the legacy
`state[:action_dim]` prefix is already correct and no code change is needed. This
avoids the bug but requires regenerating/re-normalizing the dataset.

## Important caveat

This only affects how relative actions are *computed* — it is a
**train/eval-consistency** issue. A checkpoint trained with the wrong base learned
against corrupted targets, so **fixing the map requires retraining**; it cannot be
patched at eval time alone. Eval already builds its processors from
`policy.config`, so once retrained with the correct `relative_state_index_map`,
the eval side picks it up automatically.

## Verification

Round-trip is exact with the map, and the legacy path is unchanged when it's unset:

```python
idx_map = [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
rel  = to_relative_actions(action, state, mask, idx_map)   # [[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]]
back = to_absolute_actions(rel, state, mask, idx_map)
assert torch.allclose(back, action)                         # passes
```
factor_evidence_quote: state_offset = state[..., :dims] * mask_t   # <-- assumes prefix alignment
phase_evidence_quote: eval produces wrong absolute actions
symptom_evidence_quote: the policy ends up commanding the wrong joint positions (in our case, consistently missing grasps).
title: Relative actions assume state[:action_dim] aligns with action — support explicit/name-based state→action mapping

The same on my side. OpenPi uses delta actions while LeRobot uses absolute actions. Therefore, OpenPi actions start pretty much at (0,0,0...) for each action chunk, while LeRobot's action chunk start may deviate a lot from the previous.

# Upstream Issue Draft — action-smoothing-ema-clip

**Title:** Post-hoc EMA smoothing and velocity clipping for rollout actions

## Motivation

SmolVLA (or other policy model) produces per-frame prediction noise that causes high-frequency jitter at inference. This is bad for consistent observations in fine-controled tasks, also wears out servo gears fast. This low-pass filter on commanded goal positions eliminates jitter without retraining. Actions are absolute goal positions (degrees for SO-101).

## Proposed solution

EMA smoothing + per-joint velocity clipping on commanded goal positions, applied just before `send_action` in the shared `send_next_action` dispatch function (covers all rollout strategies).

CLI-configurable via `RolloutConfig`:
- `--action_smoothing_enabled` (bool, default `True`)
- `--action_smoothing_alpha` (float, default `0.25`) — EMA blending factor
- `--action_smoothing_max_delta` (float, default `1.25`) — max per-frame change in action units
- `--action_smoothing_reset_threshold` (float, default `10.0`) — gap that skips EMA blending

Handles DAGGER correction boundaries correctly: `dagger.py` calls `reset_action_smoothing()` on correction resume, setting `_prev=None` so the first autonomous frame passes through cleanly (the policy just observed the current pose, so its output is near the physical position). No snap-back.

Three files changed:
- `rollout/configs.py` — smoothing fields on `RolloutConfig`
- `rollout/strategies/core.py` — `_smooth_action()` function + `send_next_action` wiring
- `rollout/strategies/dagger.py` — `reset_action_smoothing()` on correction resume + rollout start

## Implementation

Branch: `anikita/lerobot:feat/action-smoothing-ema-clip`
Patch: `leanton/action-smoothing-ema-clip/action-smoothing-ema-clip.diff` (209 lines, rebased on main@30790de1)

## Future work

- Constants could move from `RolloutConfig` dataclass defaults to a dedicated smoothing config group
- Periodic log (every 150 frames) could be `DEBUG` level instead of `INFO`

## Tested

On SO-101 hardware with foot pedal, SmolVLA policy, DAGGER strategy.

symptom_evidence_quote: SmolVLA (or other policy model) produces per-frame prediction noise that causes high-frequency jitter at inference.
title: Post-hoc EMA smoothing and velocity clipping for rollout actions

body:
## Description

After a DAGGER correction (CORRECTING → PAUSED → AUTONOMOUS), the RTC engine's `_obs_holder` still contains the **pre-correction observation**. The smooth handover in #3506 correctly resets the engine and interpolator at the AUTONOMOUS transition, but the RTC background thread reads the stale observation and predicts its first action chunk assuming the arm is still at its pre-correction pose. This causes a rapid snap-back toward the old position on resume.

## Reproduction

1. Run DAGGER rollout with RTC inference on actuated hardware (SO-101 leader + follower)
2. During autonomous mode, press F10 (pause) → F11 (correction)
3. Move the arm significantly away from its pre-correction position
4. Press F11 (end correction) → F10 (resume autonomous)
5. Observe: arm snaps toward the pre-correction position before smoothly continuing

## Root Cause

In `dagger.py` `_apply_transition()`, the `PAUSED → AUTONOMOUS` branch (line 731):

```python
elif new_phase == DAggerPhase.AUTONOMOUS:
    interpolator.reset()
    engine.reset()        # clears action queue, resets policy
    engine.resume()       # RTC thread wakes up, reads _obs_holder...
```

During the correction, `notify_observation()` is never called (the correction loop uses teleop actions directly). So `_obs_holder` still holds the last autonomous observation from before the pause. After `engine.reset()` + `engine.resume()`, the RTC thread reads this stale observation and produces actions that target the pre-correction state.

## Fix

Feed a fresh robot observation to the engine after reset, before resume:

```python
elif new_phase == DAggerPhase.AUTONOMOUS:
    interpolator.reset()
    engine.reset()
    # Feed fresh observation so first action chunk reflects
    # the current (post-correction) state
    fresh_obs = robot.get_observation()
    obs_processed = ctx.processors.robot_observation_processor(fresh_obs)
    engine.notify_observation(obs_processed)
    engine.resume()
```

## Environment

- LeRobot: `origin/main` at `49755a3d` (post-#3506)
- Hardware: SO-101 follower + SO-101 leader
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04, CUDA
- Inference: RTC, execution_horizon=10, fps=15

## Patch

The 4-line fix is available as a git diff — happy to open a PR if this approach looks correct.

### Ticket Type

🐛 Bug Report (Something isn't working)

### Environment & System Info

```Shell
lerobot=0.5.2 python=3.12 os=ubuntu22.04
```

### Description

## Summary

When `ActionInterpolator` is used (`interpolation_multiplier > 1`) on action vectors
whose EE orientation is encoded as a rotation vector / axis-angle (`wx, wy, wz`),
two consecutive policy actions whose rotvecs happen to be **antipodal twins**
(i.e. `r` and `r' = (2π − ‖r‖) · (−r̂)`, both representing nearly the same physical
rotation but lying ~`2π` apart in 3-vector space) produce intermediate
interpolated sub-actions that **sweep through identity rotation**. The gripper
visibly tumbles ~180° in a few control ticks. Downstream IK converts these
non-physical intermediate poses into ~90°/tick joint deltas, which the servo
silently velocity-limits and partially executes — the arm appears to stall for
a second or two and then lurch.

### Context & Reproduction

Observed on G2 dual-arm with a pi0.5 finetuned policy.
--fps=6 --interpolation_multiplier=5
--policy.use_relative_actions=true
--inference.type=rtc --inference.rtc.execution_horizon=10

A single rollout window shows two adjacent policy chunk steps with right-arm
rotvecs:
step k:   ( +1.45, -0.14, +2.34 )   ‖r‖ ≈ 2.74  (≈ 157°)
step k+1: ( -1.72, -0.38, -2.31 )   ‖r‖ ≈ 2.93  (≈ 168°)

The vector distance ‖r_{k+1} − r_k‖ ≈ 5.6 rad, but the **true angular distance**
between the rotations is only ≈ 0.6 rad — they are antipodal twins of the same
nearby orientation. With `multiplier=5`, `ActionInterpolator.add()` linearly
blends them:

| t | interpolated rotvec | ‖r‖ |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | (+0.78, −0.16, +1.38) | 1.59 |
| 0.4 | (+0.16, −0.22, +0.46) | **0.51** |
| 0.6 | (−0.46, −0.28, −0.46) | 0.74 |
| 0.8 | (−1.08, −0.34, −1.38) | 1.79 |

The dip to **‖r‖ = 0.51** means the intermediate sub-action represents a rotation
of ~29°, i.e. the gripper is asked to rotate from 157° through ~30° back to 168°
in five control ticks — a physical impossibility.

A real rollout log shows the identical signature in the `r.ee.w*` sequence sent
to IK: `‖r‖ = 2.74, 2.71, 2.66, 2.60, 2.55, 1.21, 0.34, 1.55, 2.93` over ten
consecutive 30 Hz ticks. IK then produces 90°+ joint deltas which the GDK servo
silently rejects/clamps (returns `kSuccess`, arm barely moves), then the
visually observed lurch happens once the policy moves on.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/12c87fda-41e7-4b65-a7b9-6817f4d9a2b2

### Relevant logs or stack trace

body:
### Ticket Type

🐛 Bug Report (Something isn't working)

### Environment & System Info

Hardware and host runtime:

- Host OS: `Linux 3.10.0-957.el7.x86_64 #1 SMP Thu Nov 8 23:39:32 UTC 2018`
- Slurm node: `x86_64`, `2` sockets, `32` cores/socket, `2` threads/core, `128` logical CPUs, `2060000M` real memory, `gpu:8`
- CPU: `Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8358P CPU @ 2.60GHz`
- GPU: `8 x NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB` per node
- GPU driver: `550.90.07`, CUDA runtime: `12.4`

Container and Python runtime:

- Container OS: Debian GNU/Linux 12 (`bookworm`)
- Python: `3.12.13`

<details>
<summary>Key package versions</summary>

| Package | Version |
| --- | --- |
| `torch` | `2.7.0+cu118` |
| PyTorch CUDA build | `11.8` |
| cuDNN reported by PyTorch | `90100` |
| `torchvision` | `0.22.0+cu118` |
| `transformers` | `5.4.0` |
| `triton` | `3.3.0` |
| `pytest` | `8.4.2` |
| `accelerate` | `1.13.0` |
| `datasets` | `4.8.4` |
| `huggingface_hub` | `1.10.2` |
| `safetensors` | `0.7.0` |
| `tokenizers` | `0.22.2` |
| `numpy` | `2.2.6` |
| `scipy` | `1.17.1` |
| `pillow` | `12.2.0` |

| `opencv-python` | `4.13.0.92` |
| `einops` | `0.8.2` |

</details>

### Description

LeRobot's current `transformers-dep` lower bound allows `transformers==5.4.0`, which contains a Qwen2.5-VL still-image RoPE index bug: still images can be routed through the video temporal-scaling path in `get_rope_index`, so image-token temporal positions are multiplied by `tokens_per_second` while height/width positions remain unscaled.

This silently changes Qwen2.5-VL image-token RoPE phases and can severely degrade Qwen2.5-VL-based robot policies such as `wallx` and `eo1`.

Policy-level regression of `eo1` observed on Libero (average success drops by `23.30625` points):

| code version | Libero spatial | Libero object | Libero goal | Libero 10 | average |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `transformers 4.56.0` | `100.0` | `98.8` | `98.1` | `90.6` | `96.9` |
| `transformers 5.4.0` | `55.0` | `65.0` | `86.875` | `87.50` | `73.59375` |


This matches Transformers issue [#45325](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/45325). The upstream fix is PR [#45330](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/45330), released in Transformers [v5.5.4](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/releases/tag/v5.5.4).

The vulnerable v5.4.0 code applies temporal scaling to both images and videos:

```python
time_interval = tokens_per_second * int(next(second_per_grid_ts))
```

The fixed code applies that scaling only to videos:

```python
if modality_type == 2:
    time_interval = tokens_per_second * int(next(second_per_grid_ts))
else:
    time_interval = 1
```

For VLA policies, this matters because robot observations are usually still camera frames, not videos. In a local EO1 trace with two camera images, we control the raw data, processor outputs, image tensors, token layout, and action span, but the image-token temporal axis drifts:

| image span | token span | expected temporal origin | buggy temporal origin | height/width origin |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| first image | `[16, 97)` | `16` | `32` | `16` |
| second image | `[99, 180)` | `27` | `54` | `27` |

Local trace facts:

- `position_ids` shape is `[3, 8, 221]`.
- `diff_count = 1296`.
- Differences appear only on axis `0`, the temporal/text axis.
- Height and width axes are identical.

The canonical Qwen forward path also produces the same shifted still-image RoPE semantics:

| comparison | max_abs | mean_abs |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| old `position_ids` vs new `compute_3d_position_ids()` | `27.0` | `5.2534` |
| old `position_ids` vs new native `get_rope_index()` | `27.0` | `5.2534` |
| new `compute_3d_position_ids()` vs new native `get_rope_index()` | `0` | `0` |

After the wrong RoPE positions are consumed by attention, the drift accumulates through the Qwen decoder and reaches the action head:

| tensor | max_abs | mean_abs |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `decoder_layer_00/input_hidden_states` | `0.5` | `0.00941` |
| `decoder_layer_00/output_hidden_states` | `2.3125` | `0.09074` |
| `decoder_layer_18/output_hidden_states` | `192.0` | `0.29540` |
| `decoder_layer_35/output_hidden_states` | `488.0` | `1.29809` |
| `qwen_forward_00/forward/last_hidden_state` | `36.53125` | `0.29315` |
| `eo1/action_out_proj_00/forward/output` | `2.1573` | `0.06862` |
| `forward/loss` | `0.19506` | `0.19506` |

> [!NOTE]
> In short: image tokens are present and spatially aligned, but their temporal RoPE phase is wrong. The error is then amplified by attention and changes action prediction.

### Context & Reproduction

I ran the same minimal script twice in the same container: once with `transformers==5.4.0`, and once with `transformers==5.5.4`. The check is CPU-only and does not instantiate model weights; it only loads the Qwen2.5-VL processor/config and calls `get_rope_index`.

Command:

```bash
python repro_qwen2_5_vl_rope_index.py
```

<details>
<summary>repro_qwen2_5_vl_rope_index.py</summary>

```python
import os

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
import torch
from transformers import Qwen2_5_VLConfig, Qwen2_5_VLProcessor, __version__ as transformers_version
from transformers.models.qwen2_5_vl.modeling_qwen2_5_vl import Qwen2_5_VLModel


class DummyQwen2_5VLModel:
    get_rope_index = Qwen2_5_VLModel.get_rope_index
    get_vision_position_ids = Qwen2_5_VLModel.get_vision_position_ids

    def __init__(self, config):
        self.config = config


def contiguous_spans(index):
    breaks = (index[1:] != index[:-1] + 1).nonzero().flatten() + 1
    chunks = torch.tensor_split(index, breaks.tolist())
    return [(int(chunk[0]), int(chunk[-1]) + 1) for chunk in chunks if len(chunk)]


model_id = os.environ.get("QWEN25VL_MODEL", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct")
processor = Qwen2_5_VLProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
config = Qwen2_5_VLConfig.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = DummyQwen2_5VLModel(config)

image = Image.fromarray(np.zeros((448, 448, 3), dtype=np.uint8))
prompt = (
    "<|im_start|>user\n"
    "<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>"
    "<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>"
    " predict the robot action<|im_end|>\n"
    "<|im_start|>assistant\n"
)
inputs = processor(
    text=[prompt],
    images=[image, image],
    return_tensors="pt",
    return_mm_token_type_ids=True,
)

# `get_rope_index` accepts `**kwargs`, so processor fields unrelated to RoPE
# such as `pixel_values` are ignored.
position_ids, _ = model.get_rope_index(**inputs)
image_positions = (inputs["mm_token_type_ids"][0] == 1).nonzero(as_tuple=False).flatten()

print(f"transformers={transformers_version}, tokens_per_second={config.vision_config.tokens_per_second}")
for span_id, (start, end) in enumerate(contiguous_spans(image_positions)):
    temporal = int(position_ids[0, 0, start])
    height = int(position_ids[1, 0, start])
    width = int(position_ids[2, 0, start])
    print(
        f"image_span={span_id}, token_span=[{start},{end}), "
        f"temporal={temporal}, height={height}, width={width}, "
        f"aligned={temporal == height == width}"
    )
```

</details>

Expected invariant for still images:

```python
temporal_start == height_start == width_start
```

### Relevant logs or stack trace

The same two-image still-frame prompt gives different RoPE starts:

| transformers | tokens_per_second | image_span | token_span | temporal_start | height_start | width_start | aligned |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `5.4.0` | `2` | `0` | `[4,260)` | `8` | `4` | `4` | no |
| `5.4.0` | `2` | `1` | `[262,518)` | `44` | `22` | `22` | no |
| `5.5.4` | `2` | `0` | `[4,260)` | `4` | `4` | `4` | yes |
| `5.5.4` | `2` | `1` | `[262,518)` | `22` | `22` | `22` | yes |

Summary:

- In `transformers==5.4.0`, still-image `temporal_start` is scaled by `tokens_per_second=2`.
- In `transformers==5.5.4`, `temporal_start`, `height_start`, and `width_start` are aligned for both still-image spans.

Possible fix options:

- Move LeRobot's `transformers-dep` bound to `"transformers>=5.4.0,<5.6.0"`
- Add an explicit Qwen2.5-VL RoPE-index compatibility monkey patch in Qwen2.5-VL-based policies

Affected policy scope:

- `wallx` depends on `lerobot[transformers-dep]` and `lerobot[qwen-vl-utils-dep]`.
- `eo1` depends on `lerobot[transformers-dep]` and `lerobot[qwen-vl-utils-dep]`.

### Ticket Type

🐛 Bug Report (Something isn't working)

### Environment & System Info

```Shell
OS: Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie)
  - Kernel: Linux 6.12.75 (Raspberry Pi aarch64)
  - Python: 3.13.5                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  - lerobot: 0.4.3
```

### Description

Bug: `SOFollower.configure()` sets P_Coefficient=16 (half of motor factory
default 32). With P=16, the PID output torque is insufficient to overcome
static friction when position error is small, creating a dead-band. As a
result, commanding the same goal position from different approach directions
lands the arm at different physical positions.

This breaks:
  - Reproducibility of commanded joint configurations
  - Training data accuracy (recorded actual positions differ from commanded)
  - Policy deployment (trained-on positions not reachable at eval)

This script demonstrates the bug using the standard robot API (send_action /
get_observation) and shows that P=32 (factory default) fixes it.

Hardware: SO-ARM100 (Feetech STS3215 motors)
Tested with: lerobot 0.4.3, Python 3.13

### Context & Reproduction

1. command position x on shoulder_pan
2. wait
3. Read position the motor settled at. 
4. Its not normally the target values because the p =16 runs out of juice. 

### Relevant logs or stack trace

```Shell

```

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing tickets to ensure this isn't a duplicate.
- [x] I am using the latest version of the `main` branch.
- [x] I have verified this is not an environment-specific problem.

### Additional Info / Workarounds

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Reproduction script for position accuracy issue with SO-ARM100 + lerobot.

Bug: `SOFollower.configure()` sets P_Coefficient=16 (half of motor factory
default 32). With P=16, the PID output torque is insufficient to overcome
static friction when position error is small, creating a dead-band. As a
result, commanding the same goal position from different approach directions
lands the arm at different physical positions.

This breaks:
  - Reproducibility of commanded joint configurations
  - Training data accuracy (recorded actual positions differ from commanded)
  - Policy deployment (trained-on positions not reachable at eval)

This script demonstrates the bug using the standard robot API (send_action /
get_observation) and shows that P=32 (factory default) fixes it.

Hardware: SO-ARM100 (Feetech STS3215 motors)
Tested with: lerobot 0.4.x, Python 3.13

Usage:
    # Ensure arm is powered on and calibrated
    python3 lerobot_pid_issue.py
"""

import time

from lerobot.robots.so_follower import SOFollower, SOFollowerRobotConfig


def send_and_read(robot, motor, target, settle=1.0):
    """Use the standard robot API: send_action / get_observation."""
    action = {f"{motor}.pos": target}
    robot.send_action(action)
    time.sleep(settle)
    obs = robot.get_observation()
    return obs[f"{motor}.pos"]


def test_approach(robot, motor, target, approach_positions):
    """For each approach position, go there first, then to target. Measure error."""
    results = []
    for name, approach_pos in approach_positions.items():
        # Go to approach
        send_and_read(robot, motor, approach_pos)
        # Go to target
        actual = send_and_read(robot, motor, target)
        err = actual - target
        results.append((name, target, actual, err))
    return results


def set_pid_all(robot, p=None, i=None, d=None):
    """Set PID coefficients on all motors (direct bus write)."""
    for mot in robot.bus.motors:
        if p is not None:
            robot.bus.write("P_Coefficient", mot, p)
        if i is not None:
            robot.bus.write("I_Coefficient", mot, i)
        if d is not None:
            robot.bus.write("D_Coefficient", mot, d)


def main():
    config = SOFollowerRobotConfig(port="/dev/ttyACM0", id=None)
    robot = SOFollower(config)
    robot.connect()

    try:
        motor = "shoulder_pan"
        target = 0.0  # center of normalized range (-100..+100)
        approaches = {
            "low":  -20.0,  # approach target from below
            "high": +20.0,  # approach target from above
        }

        # ─── Part 1: lerobot default (P=16) ───
        print("=" * 60)
        print("Part 1: P=16 (lerobot default)")
        print("=" * 60)
        for mot in robot.bus.motors:
            print(f"  {mot}: P={robot.bus.read('P_Coefficient', mot)}")

        print(f"\nCommanding {motor} to {target:.1f} from 2 approach directions:")
        results_p16 = test_approach(robot, motor, target, approaches)
        for name, tgt, act, err in results_p16:
            print(f"  from {name:5s}: commanded={tgt:+.1f} actual={act:+.2f} error={err:+.2f}")
        errors_p16 = [r[3] for r in results_p16]
        spread_p16 = max(errors_p16) - min(errors_p16)
        print(f"  -> Spread: {spread_p16:.2f} (normalized units, range is ±100)")

        # ─── Part 2: P=32 (motor factory default) ───
        print("\n" + "=" * 60)
        print("Part 2: P=32 (motor factory default)")
        print("=" * 60)
        set_pid_all(robot, p=32)
        time.sleep(0.2)
        for mot in robot.bus.motors:
            print(f"  {mot}: P={robot.bus.read('P_Coefficient', mot)}")

        print(f"\nCommanding {motor} to {target:.1f} from 2 approach directions:")
        results_p32 = test_approach(robot, motor, target, approaches)
        for name, tgt, act, err in results_p32:
            print(f"  from {name:5s}: commanded={tgt:+.1f} actual={act:+.2f} error={err:+.2f}")
        errors_p32 = [r[3] for r in results_p32]
        spread_p32 = max(errors_p32) - min(errors_p32)
        print(f"  -> Spread: {spread_p32:.2f} (normalized units, range is ±100)")

        # ─── Summary ───
        print("\n" + "=" * 60)
        print("Summary")
        print("=" * 60)
        print(f"P=16 spread: {spread_p16:.2f}")
        print(f"P=32 spread: {spread_p32:.2f}")
        print(f"Improvement: {spread_p16 / max(spread_p32, 0.01):.1f}x tighter with P=32")


    finally:
        # Restore lerobot's default P=16 before disconnect
        set_pid_all(robot, p=16)
        robot.disconnect()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

comments.author: rylinjames
comments.body: good catch. the p=16 default in `SOFollower.configure()` being half the feetech sts3215 factory default of 32 is real, and the dead-band from direction-dependent static friction is exactly what you'd expect at low kp. your repro with send_action + get_observation reading settled position from two approach directions is the cleanest way to show it. worth filing as a PR bumping the default to 32 (or exposing it as a config field with 32 as default), since the current value silently breaks training-data accuracy for anyone on so-arm100. reflex doesn't touch the motor-layer config, so this isn't our fix to ship, but it's a real bug and the PR should land fast. fwiw we're building reflex-vla (deploy layer for so-arm / lerobot policies on jetson). github.com/rylinjames/reflex-vla has good-first-issues tagged, or dm romirj on discord / playindus@gmail.com for collaborator access.

comments.author: jashshah999
comments.body:
Hardware positioning errors mean systematic noise in your recorded data. `lerobot-doctor check --checks actions,anomalies` can quantify positional error across episodes by detecting unusual action variance patterns. Helps decide whether to re-record.

https://github.com/jashshah999/lerobot-doctor

comments.author: 0o8o0-blip
comments.body:
Oh nice this might be fun. So you are proposing do two collections
1. with p = 16 
2. with p = 32
then train both and see performance also use your `lerobot-dcotor` tool to see if it predicts bad data ?

That could be a fun experiment to see how effected this is. Let me try that and report back.

comments.author: 0o8o0-blip
comments.body:
Okay so i did a collection with p=16 and p=32. The were 63 and 26.7 ticks from target respectively. I ran through robot dr to see if it would see differences in the data sets for quality. But it didn't.

If you wanted to detect this from data alone, you'd need a custom check that computes per-target settle position variance — i.e., for each nominal target tick, plot the distribution of actual final joint positions. P=16 would show a bimodal distribution split by approach direction; P=32 would be a tighter unimodal. That's not a check lerobot-doctor runs, but it's the kind of thing that would discriminate. Worth filing as a feature suggestion to the maintainer if   you think the broader community would care about it.

This would work for my kind of contrived use case but not sure about general usage.

comments.author: rylinjames
comments.body: the "moved a centimeter then idle" behavior on jetson orin nano with smolvla is a classic action-chunk exhaustion: the policy emits its first action chunk, the arm executes it, then either the next inference pass is too slow (orin nano + smolvla in plain pytorch is ~2-4s per forward) or the new chunk gets predicted with a stale obs and collapses to near-zero delta. pi jetson orin nano is sm_87, fp16 onnx+trt cuts smolvla inference to sub-100ms which usually unblocks this. also worth confirming: did you actually train with a dummy third camera zeroed out, or with 2 real cameras and a flag? if the model saw all-zero pixels during training it learned to condition on the zero-cam embedding, so inference-time zeros are fine, but a dim mismatch would explain idle behavior. reflex-vla does exactly the orin fp16 onnx+trt path for smolvla with cos=+1.0 parity. github.com/rylinjames/reflex-vla. good-first-issues tagged, or dm romirj on discord / playindus@gmail.com for collaborator access.

body:
### Ticket Type

🐛 Bug Report (Something isn't working)

### Environment & System Info

```Shell

```

### Description

Title: Relative-action postprocessing uses the wrong anchor state when action queue is enabled (n_action_steps > 1)

Hi team,

I found a mismatch between relative-action postprocessing and action-queue inference for ACT-like chunked policies.

## Summary

With relative actions enabled, inference should follow:

`model output (relative) -> unnormalize -> absolute conversion (relative + state_at_chunk_start) -> robot`

However, when `n_action_steps > 1` (action queue enabled), the absolute conversion is applied once per control step, and each call uses the latest cached observation state, not the state from when that chunk was predicted.

This causes wrong absolute actions for queued steps #2, #3, ... of the same chunk.

## Why this matters

Documentation says relative outputs are converted back to absolute at inference, which is correct.
But with queued chunk execution, the anchor state must remain fixed for all actions from the same chunk.
Otherwise, relative->absolute is no longer aligned with how the model produced that chunk.

## Expected behavior

For one predicted chunk, all queued relative actions should be converted to absolute using the same anchor state (the state when the chunk was generated).

## Actual behavior

Absolute conversion uses the newest cached state on every step.
So if robot state changes between dequeued actions, conversion drift appears.

## Likely root cause

- `AbsoluteActionsProcessorStep.__call__` uses `relative_step._last_state` on each postprocess call.
- `RelativeActionsProcessorStep` caches state every inference loop (even when no action exists in preprocessor input).
- `select_action` in chunked policies dequeues previously predicted actions over multiple loops.

So queued actions are converted with moving states.

## Affected places

- `src/lerobot/processor/relative_action_processor.py`
  - `RelativeActionsProcessorStep` state caching behavior
  - `AbsoluteActionsProcessorStep.__call__` uses latest cached state every call
- chunked policy `select_action` implementations using action queues (e.g., ACT/PI0-style)

## Proposal

Option A (generic, recommended):
- Add a state-hold mechanism in `AbsoluteActionsProcessorStep` (e.g., `state_hold_steps`).
- For queued action execution, reuse the same cached state for `n_action_steps` postprocess calls, then refresh.

Option B (policy-local):
- Implement an ACT-specific absolute step with state hold, without changing generic processor behavior.

## Temporary workaround

Set `n_action_steps = 1` so each action is predicted and converted in the same loop.
This avoids anchor mismatch but increases inference frequency.

Thanks!

body:
Has anyone been able to deploy the SmolVLA model to control say the SO-100 on a simulator like IsaacSim? 
Even if the fine-tuning reliably converges the observed performance on the simulator seems erratic. Do we apply the predicted actions from SmolVLA directly into the Articulation controller as positions?

comments.author: jadechoghari
comments.body:
Hi! Thanks for the question 👋

SmolVLA does not use delta actions in its default setup, it outputs absolute joint position targets (normalized during training with MEAN_STD, then unnormalized at inference). in LIBERO for example, these predicted actions are applied via a position controller, which matches the action space the model was trained on.

So if you’re deploying to IsaacSim, you’ll want to:
- unnormalize the actions before applying them.
- feed them into your articulation controller as joint position targets (not raw deltas)
- you can make sure/ base yourself that the control interface matches the LIBERO convention, otherwise the behavior may look erratic

At the end it depends on what data you want it trained on.
And tip: make sure the observation key names matches what the policy expects! you can check libero docs here: https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/en/libero
