## ❓ Questions and Help

Hi, 

I am wondering whether we could make the RGB sensor noise deterministic. Currently, the RGB noise is totally random across different runs, which makes reproducibility from using Habitat-API almost impossible if users want to try noisy setting.

For example, if we use the [PointNav config file](https://github.com/facebookresearch/habitat-challenge/blob/master/configs/challenge_pointnav2020.local.rgbd.yaml) from this year's challenge as the following:
```python
env = habitat.Env(config=config)
obs = env.reset()
```
You will not get the same `obs['rgb']` every time you try the above snippet. I guess the culprit is the `numba` parallel feature used here:
https://github.com/facebookresearch/habitat-sim/blob/9eabc8a518ef5eaa6273a43b405c88988e38a81d/habitat_sim/sensors/noise_models/gaussian_noise_model.py#L16

I am not sure to what extent it will hurt the speed if we disable it.

Do you have any suggestions? Thanks

comments.author: Skylion007
comments.body:
You have to set the `np.random.seed` and `random.seed` within the @numba.jit compiled code section to change the seed used by JIT'd code. Numba actually uses a different, faster PRNG than vanilla numpy. 

Disabling the njit for the Gaussian noise model will result in a 50X performance regression of that function, believe it or not. (PRNG is really slow in numpy).

See the code for setting the seed in [Habitat-API](https://github.com/facebookresearch/habitat-api/blob/e0807ed403902de78ee37b36766c2f06e5886fea/habitat/core/env.py#L276)

```

Meanwhile, I will have deterministic results if I set the following environment variables:
```bash

```

Therefore, I think the randomness comes from the `parallel` feature of `numba`, which makes sense since the behavior of parallelism could not be determined by setting the random seed.

I think other people also encounter similar behavior as results from this [issue](https://github.com/facebookresearch/habitat-challenge/issues/46) in the habitat-challenge repo. Similarly, I could not have consistent results no matter whether it is in local docker or local non-docker and I find RBG noises are not same across different runs.

comments.author: Skylion007
comments.body: Yes, if you want to remove all the randomness of the JIT function, then you should set 'parallel=False' and 'fastmath=False,' but that will likely cause a significant performance penalty. The underlying PRNG is likely still faster than vanilla numpy's even without parallelism. Forcing all OpenMP and MKL code to be single threaded though will likely incur performance penalties.

```

@erikwijmans Thank you so much for the code, however, I think there is a misunderstanding here, and I think I have found the reason for it, maybe you already knew about this but it is new to me so I will share here.

While your code works and provides valid coordinates on paper. Habitat simulator divides the z value in 2 parts, 1. the position of the camera with respect to the agent and 2. the position of the agent itself.
So in this case for example if I have the matterport point pt_mp3d and I follow your code it results in the point pt_habitat as follow:

```py
import habitat_sim
from habitat_sim.utils.common import quat_from_two_vectors, quat_rotate_vector
pt_mp3d = [2.345, 1.78, 1.5698]

q_habitat_mp3d = quat_from_two_vectors(np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]), habitat_sim.geo.GRAVITY)
pt_habitat = quat_rotate_vector(q_habitat_mp3d, pt_mp3d)

//**The result is the pt_habitat = [2.345, 1.5698, -1.78]**
```
**The resulting point is valid on its own, but when I input that point in the habitat simulator, the image goes to a higher position than expected.** 

For example, the image you show before is an example of that happening.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7004860/71860670-26139000-3137-11ea-8b1d-afd29a5c53cb.png)


So what is happening is that while pt_habitat = [2.345, 1.5698, -1.78] is a valid translation, the **habitat simulator divides the z value between the camera position and the position of the agent.** The camera position is fixed and it follows the dataset while the agent position z value is modified accordingly.  In summary,  Instead of using the pt_habitat after the translation, the pt_habitat should be interpreted as:

camera_position = agent_state.sensor_states["rgb"].position
z = camera_position[1] 
agent_state.position = [2.345, **1.5698 - z**, -1.78]

Since the camera position is not available at the start, I took the z values of the camera from the camera parameters in the matterport camera parameters file, I used undistorted_camera_parameters file for that. 

By using that I was able to calculate the real value of the agent position and the camera position which in this example has to be something like pt_habitat = [2.345, 0.0701, -1.78] since the camera z value was at 1.4997 according to the undistorted_camera_parameters file.

By following that procedure I was able to find the real point that is the same in both simulators.

comments.body:
> camera_position = agent_state.sensor_states["rgb"].position
z = camera_position[1]
agent_state.position = [2.345, 1.5698 - z, -1.78]

> Since the camera position is not available at the start, I took the z values of the camera from the camera parameters in the matterport camera parameters file, I used undistorted_camera_parameters file for that.

Careful with this.  The camera height in the Matterport3D simulator is not consistent (because it is not consistent in the matterport3D dataset itself), most of the time it is ~1.25m, but often higher or (a lot) lower.  Habitat allows the agent to be set to an arbitrary location (even weird/non-navigable ones) so an individual render will look fine, but moving forward will no longer work as expected.

> If the result was inf I searched a snap_point for the start_point since I know the goal should be reachable.

This assumption is wrong.  Some of the goals will no longer be reachable due to reconstruction errors -- the navigation graph in the Matterport3D simulator contains transitions that cannot be sensibly approximated in habitat-sim.

The procedure outlined seems dangerous.  I am not sure how the search procedure is done, but it seems likely that the found point which has a path to the goal will no longer be valid for the corresponding natural language instruction.

Just to clarify, `snap_point` is deterministic. i.e. `snap_point(pt) == snap_point(pt)` and if `pt` was already a navigable location, then `snap_point(pt) == pt`.   Also, it will simply find the closest navigable location to the given point and there is no way to constrain it (i.e. there is no way to tell it to try to find a point in the same connected component as another point).

Ah, if you are using teleport, then I can see how this may work.

comments.body:
Internally, we have a check to see if there is a feasible path between two points (just checking to see if two points are part of the same connect component).   That could be used to limit the agent to only be able to teleport to locations that are part of the same connect component.  We currently have https://aihabitat.org/docs/habitat-sim/habitat_sim.nav.PathFinder.html#island_radius exposed that queries part of that system.   You can use that filter things (the probability that two separate connect components have the exact same size is basically zero), i.e. `pathfinder.island_radius(current_position) == pathfinder.island_radius(teleport_position)`.

We can expose the `has_path` check if this fits your need.

## Habitat-Sim version
v0.2.1

## 🐛 Bug

The ground truth semantic camera outputs in Matterport3D environments seem to not match the environment being observed by the RGB and depth cameras. This occurs even when I use the Colab notebook `ECCV 2020: Navigation` in this repo and listed at https://aihabitat.org/tutorial/2020/.

## Steps to Reproduce

On Colab:
1. Open the notebook: https://colab.research.google.com/github/facebookresearch/habitat-sim/blob/main/examples/tutorials/colabs/ECCV_2020_Navigation.ipynb
2. Comment out the following lines at the end of the `Define Observation Display Utility Function` cell, since the import throws an error:
```
if display:
    from habitat.utils.visualizations import maps
```
3. Run all cells in sequence up until and not including the `Working with the NavMesh Cell`. This produces the following outputs, where the semantic image does not correspond with the RGB and depth ones (but it does seem to be executing the correct actions).
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/39648931/168637160-238a09a5-db69-42be-ab39-910de86a25ab.png)

Locally:
I copied and ran parts of the above notebook example into a .py script and ran it. The following code (saved as a .txt) saves the generated images to a directory called `./example_imgs`:
[test.txt](https://github.com/facebookresearch/habitat-sim/files/8701721/test.txt)

This outputs the same thing as the Colab notebook. I tried a few other environments from MP3D and they all had similar errors, where the semantic image seems to not match the RGB and depth.

See additional context for more details.

## Expected behavior

The semantic image should match that of the RGB and depth images -- see the below image, taken from https://youtu.be/kunFMRJAu2U?t=883, which ran the exact notebook I ran, with no differences.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/39648931/168636407-0af158ef-ca76-4e14-8a73-417018375f6d.png)

## Additional context
I installed `habitat-sim`'s `challenge-2022-branch`, but wanted to enable semantics for testing. This page https://github.com/facebookresearch/habitat-sim/blob/main/DATASETS.md says that I need to add a scene config file to the MP3D directory and to specify the path to it in the sim settings dictionary, which I have. However, even without the line:
```
"scene_dataset":
    "./habitat-challenge-data/data/scene_datasets/mp3d/v1/tasks/mp3d/mp3d.scene_dataset_config.json",
```
in the dictionary, everything works the same.

sim_cfg.scene_dataset_config_file = settings["scene_dataset"]

Else, the scene dataset config file path in the dictionary would not do anything.

I am leaving this topic open so that this bug can also be fixed in the notebooks in the repo though.

## 🐛 Bug
The agent goes out of bounds and the episodes ends because of segmentation fault.

## Command
I ran the example below

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

<!-- If you were running a command, post the exact command that you were running -->

1. Set the agent in a position close to a wall, for example:
**map**: data/scene_datasets/mp3d/2n8kARJN3HM/2n8kARJN3HM.navmesh
**start_pos**: [-0.20505089, -3.468762, 2.312384]
**start_rot**: quaternion(0.41104656457901, 0, 0.91161435842514,0)
2. Set the FORWARD_STEP_SIZE: 2.00
3. Trigger the "MOVE_FORWARD" action.

Those steps will make the agent fall out of bounds in the second dimension and not the first. So when the projection procedure checks for errors it cannot determine that there is a NAN in the position. Therefore the agent act method wrongly returns that there is not a collision after the action is performed. Which is in fact not true, there is a collision or the agent is "out of bounds". 

Code Sample:

` import habitat
import cv2
from habitat.sims.habitat_simulator.actions import HabitatSimActions

FORWARD_KEY="w"
LEFT_KEY="a"
RIGHT_KEY="d"
FINISH="f"


def transform_rgb_bgr(image):
    return image[:, :, [2, 1, 0]]


def example():
    print("Starting habitat Environment")
    env = habitat.Env(
        config=habitat.get_config("configs/tasks/pointnav.yaml")
    )
    print("Environment creation successful")
    observations = env.reset()
    cv2.imshow("RGB", transform_rgb_bgr(observations["rgb"]))

    print("Agent stepping around inside environment.")
   
   
    initial_state = env._sim.get_agent_state(0)
    init_translation = initial_state.position
    init_rotation = initial_state.rotation
       
    print(init_translation, init_rotation)
    print(observations["heading"])
   
    count_steps = 0
    while not env.episode_over:
        keystroke = cv2.waitKey(0)

        if keystroke == ord(FORWARD_KEY):
            action = "MOVE_FORWARD"
            print("action: FORWARD")
        elif keystroke == ord(LEFT_KEY):
            action = "TURN_LEFT"
            print("action: LEFT")
        elif keystroke == ord(RIGHT_KEY):
            action = "TURN_RIGHT"
            print("action: RIGHT")
        elif keystroke == ord(FINISH):
            action = "STOP"
            print("action: FINISH")
        else:
            print("INVALID KEY")
            continue

        observations = env.step(action)
        count_steps += 1
        print(observations["heading"])
        #print("Destination, distance: {:3f}, theta(radians): {:.2f}".format(
        #    observations["pointgoal"][0], observations["pointgoal"][1]))
        cv2.imshow("RGB", transform_rgb_bgr(observations["rgb"]))
       
        initial_state = env._sim.get_agent_state(0)
        init_translation = initial_state.position
        init_rotation = initial_state.rotation
       
        print(init_translation, init_rotation)

    print("Episode finished after {} steps.".format(count_steps))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    example()`

## Expected behavior

A collision occurs and the agent doesn't move to the void. 

## Additional context

The validation for projectToPoly should be in the three dimensions but currently is done in only one dimension. Which causes an error when walking near the walls diagonally since the resulting projection becomes ( number, NAN, number) which is not properly validated. The file in question is under **src/esp/nav/PathFinder.cpp**

`std::tuple<dtStatus, dtPolyRef, vec3f> projectToPoly(
    const T& pt,
    const dtNavMeshQuery* navQuery,
    const dtQueryFilter* filter) {
  // Defines size of the bounding box to search in for the nearest polygon.  If
  // there is no polygon inside the bounding box, the status is set to failure
  // and polyRef == 0
  constexpr float polyPickExt[3] = {2, 4, 2};  // [2 * dx, 2 * dy, 2 * dz]
  dtPolyRef polyRef;
  // Initialize with all NANs at dtStatusSucceed(status) == true does NOT mean
  // that it found a point to project to..........
  vec3f polyXYZ{NAN, NAN, NAN};
  dtStatus status = navQuery->findNearestPoly(pt.data(), polyPickExt, filter,
                                              &polyRef, polyXYZ.data());

  // So let's call it a failure if it didn't actually find a point....
  **if (std::isnan(polyXYZ[0]))
    status = DT_FAILURE;**

  return std::make_tuple(status, polyRef, polyXYZ);
}`


## System Info

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7004860/70135550-9c9f1700-16cd-11ea-966a-ff4a89994b91.png)

## Motivation and Context

Unit tests to verify physics determinism in habitat-sim Emscriptem/JS build and the native Linux/Mac build. Currently, there is no way to verify if physics is deterministic across habitat-sim builds and for every new change/build of habitat-sim we don't know if physics will be deterministic or not. Idea was to keep a test in place which we could use to verify whether physics works exactly same across habitat-sim builds with zero error in states. 

In this unit test we add two objects in stacking like scenario, where two dynamic objects are being dropped at same x, z coordinate at different heights. We keep record of all object states after every physics step and use ground truth states recorded from native build. Currently, the test is failing.

## Motivation and Context

Related to Issue #301 

Blocked by: PRs #309, #310. (diff includes these)

This PR addresses remaining physics instabilities when loading hierarchal meshes as Bullet rigid object by introducing optional but default mesh joining for more stable simulation of compound objects.

### Mesh joining:
Creating compound shapes as combinations of convex components can be an effective way of introducing macro concavities efficiently into simulation. PR #310 added this functionality by computing convex hulls for each mesh in a loaded collision mesh hierarchy and combining them into a single `btCompoundShape` object. However, when individual convex hulls overlap significantly, this treatment can result in unstable simulation artifacts. 
**This is demonstrated by simulation of a compound box shape with 2 convex sub-boxes only slightly offset from one another:** 
![cube_compound_jitter_example](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1445143/67315331-36628a00-f4bb-11e9-8c60-45577a625c3c.gif)
To remedy this, meshes can be joined into one convex hull, losing any concavity for improved stability and efficiency:

The mesh join option is added to the physics object config with default true for stability.

Local testing.

I am implementing a Ground Truth (GT) dynamics model for an MPPI planner using ManiSkill. My architecture consists of two environments:

- env_real (num_envs=1): Represents the "real world" or interaction environment.
- env_sim (num_envs=K, e.g., 2048): Used as the internal world model for MPPI to perform massive parallel rollouts.

My goal is to copy the exact state from env_real to all 2048 environments in env_sim at every planning step to ensure the rollouts start from the true current state.

Here is my current implementation
```
def dynamics_gt(state, action):
    """
    Ground Truth dynamics based on state synchronization.
    
    Args:
        state: (K, 1, nx) - Current state.
        action: (K, H, nu) - Action sequences generated by MPPI Planner.
    """
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Step 1: State Synchronization (Sync Real -> Sim)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Get the authoritative physical state from env_real
    real_state_dict = env_real.base_env.get_state_dict()

    # Apply this state to the parallel environment
    env_sim.base_env.set_state_dict(real_state_dict)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Step 2: Parallel Rollout
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    K, H, nu = action.shape
    predicted_states = []
    
    # Execute H steps in parallel on GPU
    for t in range(H):
        action_t = action[:, t, :] # (K, nu)
        
        # Step simulation
        obs, _, _, _, _ = env_sim.step(action_t)
        
        # Process observation
        predicted_states.append(obs_processed.unsqueeze(1))
    
    # Reset to clear buffers (if necessary)
    env_sim.reset(seed=0)

    # Return trajectory: (K, H, nx)
    return torch.cat(predicted_states, dim=1)
```

```
# Initialize the large environment (Sim / World Model)
env_sim = gym.make(
    "PushT-v1",
    obs_mode="state",
    control_mode="pd_ee_delta_pos",
    num_envs=NUM_SAMPLES  # e.g., 2048
)
env_sim = ManiSkillVectorEnv(env_sim, ignore_terminations=True, auto_reset=False)
env_sim.reset(seed=0) 

# Initialize the single environment (Real / Interaction)
print("Initializing env_real (1)...")
env_real = gym.make(
    "PushT-v1",
    obs_mode="state",
    control_mode="pd_ee_delta_pos",
    render_mode="rgb_array", 
    num_envs=1,
    sim_backend="physx_cuda" # Ensure backend consistency
)
env_real = ManiSkillVectorEnv(env_real, ignore_terminations=True, auto_reset=False)

# Wrapper for saving videos
env_real = RecordEpisode(
    env_real,
    output_dir="./plan_videos_gt",
    save_trajectory=False,
    save_video=True,
    video_fps=10,
    info_on_video=True
)

env_real.reset(seed=0)

```

I have observed some potential subtle inconsistencies between the env_real behavior and the env_sim rollouts. I would like to clarify the following:

- Should I expect the simulation result of env_real (step 0 to T) to be bit-wise identical to env_sim (step 0 to T) if they start from the same state? Are there known issues where parallelization introduces slight numerical divergence compared to a single-environment instance?

- Is there a better or more standard way to clone the state of a single environment into a vectorized environment for planning purposes?


Any guidance or insights on this  would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!

comments.body:
I am working with the PushT-v1 environment and encountering state synchronization and determinism issues when transferring the state from a single environment (num_envs=1) to a vectorized environment (num_envs=N, e.g., 2) using get_state_dict() and set_state_dict().

The Workflow:
- Initialize env_A (num_envs=1) and env_B (num_envs=2). Both use physx_cuda.
- Step env_A for 5 steps (warm-up) to reach a non-initial state.
- Sync state: env_B.set_state_dict(env_A.get_state_dict()).
- Run both environments for 30 steps using identical actions (broadcasting the action from A to B).

The Problem: 
I observe significant divergence in the object (T-block) pose:
- A vs B: The trajectory in env_B diverges from env_A.
- Internal Divergence in B: Surprisingly, the two parallel environments within env_B (index 0 and index 1) also diverge from each other, despite being initialized with the same state and receiving the exact same actions.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
GPU simulation should not be assumed to be deterministic unless
- The number of parallel environments is the same
- The spacing of these environments are the same
- The state encompassing all of the parallel environments (not just per env) is the same

This can be due to a number of factors including floating point errors. Each parallel env is actually simulated in one giant scene, and is just placed at different locations, so small floating point differences can accumulate and cause a difference.

Moreover, if you use a single environment you default to the physx_cpu backend, which runs different a physics engine and has no guarantee of being the same.

Some environments like PickCube don't have this problem as much (when running actions from a converged pick cube policy) since the robot grasp can be off by a little and the cube will still be grasped, and the rest of the episode the cube's pose is determined by the robot's joint angles. Robot joint angles generally do not drift / have as much error (assuming not many contacts or using an absolute controller) since at each timestep they are driven to some given joint target.

comments.author: paLeziart
comments.body:
Hello @StoneT2000 

I also encountered this issue recently in a custom environment I made. I was getting an out-of-memory issue the fourth time the eval envs were called. Like with eval freq at 250 it would trigger at iteration 750. Reducing the eval freq did not change the pattern of triggering at the fourth evaluation.

The issue suddenly appeared so I managed to easily track it down to something I had added: a call to `env.agent.robot.get_net_contact_forces(["left_ankle_link"])` in my `_get_obs_state_dict` custom function. So instead I'm computing and storing the contact forces in a class attribute inside `_after_simulation_step`, that I later access without issue in `_get_obs_state_dict`.

I assume the out-of-memory issue comes from calling the contact API during the reset of all eval envs at the start of the evaluation process. I had the issue because `get_obs` is called at the end of `reset` in BaseEnv class. Switching the API call to `_after_simulation_step` dodges the issue because it is not called during reset.

Using:
Ubuntu 24.04
NVIDIA-SMI 570.133.07
Driver Version 570.133.07
CUDA Version: 12.8
NVIDIA RTX 4090

Note that my training uses around 10 Gb out of the 24 Gb of the card so there is quite a lot of free memory.

body: Hi Has anyone managed to get a decent success rate while training the "PickCube-v1" task using 100 demonstrations for Diffusion Policy ? I managed to get results similar to the paper for the "rgb" obs (~0.75 success) but if I change it to "rgb+depth", the model is not training properly and I get success rate of less than 10 %. The training can be reproduced with the following commands- Generate demonstration data: ``` python -m mani_skill.trajectory.replay_trajectory --traj-path ~/.maniskill/demos/PickCube-v1/motionplanning/trajectory.h5 --use-first-env-state -c pd_ee_delta_pos -o rgb+depth --save-traj --num-envs 10 -b physx_cpu ``` Perform Training ``` seed=1 demos=100 python train_rgbd.py --env-id PickCube-v1 --demo-path ~/.maniskill/demos/PickCube-v1/motionplanning/trajectory.rgb+depth.pd_ee_delta_pos.physx_cpu.h5 --control-mode "pd_ee_delta_pos" --sim-backend "physx_cpu" --num-demos ${demos} --max_episode_steps 100 --total_iters 30000 --obs-mode "rgb+depth" --exp-name diffusion_policy-PickCube-v1-rgb+depth-${demos}_motionplanning_demos-${seed} --track ``` Note you might need to change this line to 'depth' instead of 'rgbd' to get the above training running https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/blob/83570f1e9fe7d5dee942e338d336cddd43d8718d/examples/baselines/diffusion_policy/train_rgbd.py#L479 Let me know if anyone has any solution. Thanks a lot Reference wandb runs Best Manthan

Ah I know what you mean. The environment states do not encode object geometry like object scale, it only ensures the poses are the same.

Currently in your code what exactly is being randomized at scene loading stage and episode initialization? Generally object geometry should and only ever be randomized in def _load_scene and when doing so you should use the `self._batched_episode_rng` object (numpy rng but batched) to ensure better reproducibility as well as reproducibility on the level object geometry randomization between CPU and GPU sim when resetting with the same seeds.

RNG and reproducibility is tricky given users may randomize just about anything, I recommend learning more about RNG here: https://maniskill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/concepts/rng.html

comments.body:
Hi @StoneT2000 

I am having some issues with reproducibility in GPU parallelized environments. For testing purposes, I am evaluating a policy on the same initial condition 30 times in parallel. How do I use _batched_episode_rng? Since it is a private variable, I assumed that the function call to reset with a seed list should resolve the randomness across parallel environments:

```
def reset(self, seed: Union[None, int, list[int]] = None, options: Union[None, dict] = None):
        """Reset the ManiSkill environment with given seed(s) and options. Typically seed is either None (for unseeded reset) or an int (seeded reset).
        For GPU parallelized environments you can also pass a list of seeds for each parallel environment to seed each one separately.

        If options["env_idx"] is given, will only reset the selected parallel environments. If
        options["reconfigure"] is True, will call self._reconfigure() which deletes the entire physx scene and reconstructs everything.
        Users building custom tasks generally do not need to override this function.

        Returns the first observation and a info dictionary. The info dictionary is of type


        .. highlight:: python
        .. code-block:: python

            {
                "reconfigure": bool # (True if the env reconfigured. False otherwise)
            }



        Note that ManiSkill always holds two RNG states, a main RNG, and an episode RNG. The main RNG is used purely to sample an episode seed which
        helps with reproducibility of episodes and is for internal use only. The episode RNG is used by the environment/task itself to
        e.g. randomize object positions, randomize assets etc. Episode RNG is accessible by using `self._batched_episode_rng` which is numpy based and `torch.rand`
        which can be used to generate random data on the GPU directly and is seeded. Note that it is recommended to use `self._batched_episode_rng`
        if you need to ensure during reconfiguration the same objects are loaded. Reproducibility and seeding when there is GPU and CPU simulation can be tricky and we recommend reading
        the documentation for more recommendations and details on RNG https://maniskill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/concepts/rng.html

        Upon environment creation via gym.make, the main RNG is set with fixed seeds of 2022 to 2022 + num_envs - 1 (seed is just 2022 if there is only one environment)
        During each reset call, if seed is None, main RNG is unchanged and an episode seed is sampled from the main RNG to create the episode RNG.
        If seed is not None, main RNG is set to that seed and the episode seed is also set to that seed. This design means the main RNG determines
        the episode RNG deterministically.

        """
```

So, I am calling the reset function to each parallel environment with the same seed:

`obs, info = env.reset(options=eval_env_config, seed=[cfg.seed for k in range(env_cfg.num_envs)])`

However, this still results in different evaluation outcomes for the same policy. I have made sure that the policy is deterministic.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
_batched_episode_rng is slower typically (its a literal list of numpy RNG objects). It is used typically for reconfiguration time (def _load_scene and def _load_agent) (doesn't always occur during a reset) randomizations, which means object geometries, sizes, textures etc. usually (depends on how the task is written).

However the task initialization (def _initialize_episode) always occurs each env reset, so it needs to be relatively faster, so _batched_episode_rng is not used and instead torch random is typically used to generate batched numbers faster.

If you really want the initial state to be the same use env.set_state_dict(some_state_dict). State dict is retrieved via env.get_state_dict() and will be batched in dict leaves by number of parallel environments. This state setting method also lets you run things mostly deterministically in GPU sim even with a different number of parallel environments than the one used to get the state dict originally. This strategy is used for trajectory replay, as torch RNG is not element wise reproducible (so a different number of parallel envs will always yield different initial states).

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
Pull the latest code from Maniskill main branch (or wait for pypi release) and make sure to redownload the YCB dataset:

```
python -m mani_skill.utils.download_asset ycb
```

The following should work, im noticing for seed 9351 training success once hits around 80%
```
seeds=(9351 4796 1788)
for seed in ${seeds[@]}
do
  python ppo_fast.py --env_id="PickSingleYCB-v1" --seed=${seed} \
    --num_envs=4096 --num-steps=16 --update_epochs=8 --num_minibatches=32 \
    --total_timesteps=50_000_000 \
    --num_eval_envs=16 \
    --cudagraphs --exp-name="ppo-PickSingleYCB-v1-state-${seed}-walltime_efficient" \
    --track
done
```

I am not sure when you copied our ppo.py code but there is an important thing you should be aware of which is to turn off finite_horizon_gae. I find it gives better performance coupled with high number of parallel environments and fewer steps per environment in each (before we used to do --num-steps=50 but we now typically use 16 and it works well). I also recommend using the ppo_fast.py code which is basically the exact same but has experimental cudagraphs support which enables faster training.

Generally setting seed should be nearly completely reproducible.

Is there an example of this occurring, our tests usually check for this

comments.author: TritiumR

Thanks for the reply. I mean there is some divergence among the paralleled sub-scene as shown here. The states are set to the state of first sub-scene and the actions are same.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c3aa08b6-ec80-45e6-ace6-6c54669267e6

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
Generally there is always some non-determinism due to likely floating point precisions causing small things to lead to larger divergences over longer periods of time. I think if you rerun the code it is reproducible within parallel env, but beyond not necessarily

Internally what really is happening is the e.g. object at position (x, y, z), is really in one big scene with position (x + sx, y + sy, z) where sx, sy is the origin of the subscene. There can be small minute differences here.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
Ok it looks like the issue is clear, you have some self collisions that you want to disable (you don't need to disable all of them).

There are two options here:

1. If you want to keep as many collision meshes as possible (to be close to the real robot)
- You can first check which collision meshes are colliding with which, and then disable those specifically either with code or use a .srdf file (see the fetch robot for how it works). You can check during runtime with the viewer which collisions are occuring and if you notice a pair that shouldn't collide add the pair of links that are colliding to the .srdf file:
![debugging-collisions](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/16bf337c-2980-4ffa-a5bc-641dc3b27707)
2. Keep your current simplified setup with the bad collisions commented out. This will speed up simulation and is easier to do (it already works for you). Just know that objects can e.g. pass through the palm of the hand now. But sometimes for some tasks this is fine because you might want to only use the e.g. fingers.

comments.author: CreativeNick
comments.body: I don't have an .srdf file for my bimanual allegro hand robot. Would it be best to create one for the sake of using the first option to debug this? I don't want to do the second option since I plan on training the model to apply it to a real world robot.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body: You have to disable some self collisions regardless unless you fine tune the collision meshes a lot. To avoid disabling all of them the .srdf can define which specific pairs of collisions to ignore.

After private discussion with the original poster, the conclusion is as follows so far

The scores on the leaderboard are indeed correct and the leaderboard is evaluating submissions correctly. The problem lies in the user_solution.py file which leverages ManiSkill2-Learn. Currently OpenCabinetDoor and the other ManiSkill1 environments do not return agent base_pose values to the observation. To address that the ManiSkill2-Learn framework automatically adds it by using the actual environment's robot information. 

However, in submissions, the user_solution.py file creates a dummy environment to process observations which includes adding the base_pose. This dummy environment is not the actual environment so there is a mismatch in results as running the ManiSkill2-Learn evaluation will produce successes but running the actual evaluation where there is no access to the actual environment will cause errors as the base_pose values are wrong (and this is also why the robot looks like its only going one direction, the observation is not really changing)

We are currently discussing fixes for this.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
for

```
python -m mani_skill.trajectory.replay_trajectory  --traj-path=/demos/PushCube-v1/motionplanning/trajectory.h5 -c pd_ee_pose -o state_dict 
```

I am not having any significant issues, I am able to replay almost all of the demos. This entirely can be due to some small amount of in-determinism e.g. using a different machine. Different machines will sometimes have very slightly different numerical results.

For the traj.cuda.h5 file it sounds like you might have some outdated files. Trajectories generated in parallel GPU sim should have the extension `.physx_cuda.h5`. 

If you check the recommended replay scripts for e.g. imitation learning workflows here https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/blob/main/scripts/data_generation/replay_for_il_baselines.sh (docs for IL that you should read are here as well: https://maniskill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/learning_from_demos/setup.html)

we have the following script you should run to replay PushT-v1

```
python -m mani_skill.utils.download_demo PushT-v1
python -m mani_skill.trajectory.replay_trajectory \
  --traj-path ~/.maniskill/demos/PushT-v1/rl/trajectory.none.pd_ee_delta_pose.physx_cuda.h5 \
  --use-env-states -c pd_ee_delta_pose -o state \
  --save-traj --num-envs 1024 -b physx_cuda
```

this works fine. Notice that we add --use-env-states for PushT-v1 (and only for that task) since the task has a lot of constant and dynamic contacts that on any rerun on a GPU sim can easily deviate and never replay correctly with just pure actions (GPU sim is not guaranteed to be deterministic, can depend on machine, number of parallel envs etc.)

I recommend deleting the old demos and redownloading. Furthermore try using ManiSkill b21 version or nightly, both should be fine.

comments.body:
This seems like a strange error. Could you try running this script first? it's a barebones demo script that tests video generation:

```
python -m mani_skill.examples.demo_random_action -e "PickCube-v1" \
  --render-mode="rgb_array" --record-dir="videos"
```

body:
Hi, I am wondering if it is possible to disable part of the collision in the sim?
E.g., if I loaded two URDFs:
```
        loader = self.scene.create_urdf_loader()
        loader.fix_root_link = False
        loader.name = "hammer_grasp"
        self.hammer_grasp = loader.load(self.hammer_grasp_urdf_path)
        self.hammer_grasp_handel = self.hammer_grasp.links_map["handle_link"]

        loader = self.scene.create_urdf_loader()
        loader.fix_root_link = True
        loader.name = "hammer_tgt"
        self.hammer_tgt = loader.load(self.hammer_tgt_urdf_path)
        self.hammer_tgt_handel = self.hammer_tgt.links_map["handle_link"]
```

And I just want to disable the collision between self.hammer_grasp and self.hammer_tgt, but still make them colliding/contacting with other objects, is it possible?

One more follow up question: Is it possible to "fix" an object (equivalent to creating a fixed joint) to the robot hand, once there are contact forces between the finger link and the specified link, e.g., I am using this to evaluate grasping, is it possible to attach the object to hand in this function?
```
    def is_grasping(
        self,
        object: Actor,  # pylint: disable=redefined-builtin
        min_force: float = 50.0,
        max_angle: int = 60,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        """Check if the robot is grasping an object.

        Args:
            object (Actor): The object to check if the robot is grasping
            min_force (float, optional): Minimum force before the robot is
                considered to be grasping the object in Newtons. Defaults to 30.0.
            max_angle (int, optional): Maximum angle of contact to consider grasping. Defaults to 60.
        """
        l_contact_forces = self.scene.get_pairwise_contact_forces(
            self.finger1_link, object
        )
        r_contact_forces = self.scene.get_pairwise_contact_forces(
            self.finger2_link, object
        )
        lforce = torch.linalg.norm(l_contact_forces, axis=1)
        rforce = torch.linalg.norm(r_contact_forces, axis=1)

        # direction to open the gripper
        ldirection = self.finger1_link.pose.to_transformation_matrix()[..., :3, 2]
        langle = common.compute_angle_between(ldirection, l_contact_forces)
        lflag = torch.logical_and(
            lforce >= min_force, torch.rad2deg(langle) <= max_angle
        )
        rdirection = -self.finger2_link.pose.to_transformation_matrix()[..., :3, 2]
        rangle = common.compute_angle_between(rdirection, r_contact_forces)
        rflag = torch.logical_and(
            rforce >= min_force, torch.rad2deg(rangle) <= max_angle
        )
        return torch.logical_and(lflag, rflag)
```

Thanks!

comments.body:
There currently is not a straight forward way to attach an object to another. One way to do so is to create a joint between two separate links, and change its PD parameters. When both are 0, they don't affect each other, when set to large number they will try and stick together. I don't have a good API design for this.

For disabling collisions its possible. See

https://maniskill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/mani_skill/utils/structs/actor/index.html#mani_skill.utils.structs.actor.Actor.set_collision_group_bit

https://maniskill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/mani_skill/utils/structs/link/index.html#mani_skill.utils.structs.link.Link.set_collision_group

Essentially make sure the two parts you don't want to collide share the same true bit at the same index in collision group 2.

If you look at the attached source code for those 2 functions you can see how to also control the collision filtering at the per-shape level.

I wish collision disabling was a easy problem. Unfortunately this is what we are given with physx and we cannot simply do something like `self.scene.disable_contacts(actor_1, actor_2)` due to physx collision filtering mechanism

(I had an idea of trying to collect all the pairs of contacts a user wants to disable, and then generate collision bits for each actor/link/shape, but turns out that problem might be NP-hard since it requires using the other non-intuitive collision groups and becomes a graph theory problem probably)

    def _add_ycb_links_to_builder(self, builder):
        """Add YCB object as 6-DOF link chain to the articulation builder.

        Args:
            builder: ArticulationBuilder to modify
        """
        # Find the hand_frame link builder
        hand_link_builder = None
        for link_builder in builder.link_builders:
            if link_builder.name == self.ee_link_name:
                hand_link_builder = link_builder
                break

        if hand_link_builder is None:
            raise ValueError(f"Could not find '{self.ee_link_name}' in URDF")

        # Define 6 joints: 3 prismatic (XYZ) + 3 revolute (roll, pitch, yaw)
        joint_configs = [
            ("prismatic_x", "prismatic", "x", [-2.0, 2.0]),
            ("prismatic_y", "prismatic", "y", [-2.0, 2.0]),
            ("prismatic_z", "prismatic", "z", [-2.0, 2.0]),
            ("revolute_roll", "revolute", "x", [-np.pi, np.pi]),
            ("revolute_pitch", "revolute", "y", [-np.pi, np.pi]),
            ("revolute_yaw", "revolute", "z", [-np.pi, np.pi]),
        ]

        current_parent = hand_link_builder

        # Create 5 dummy links (for first 5 joints)
        for i, (joint_name, joint_type, _, limits) in enumerate(joint_configs[:-1]):
            dummy_link = builder.create_link_builder(current_parent)
            dummy_link.set_name(f"ycb_dummy_{i}")

            # Minimal mass and inertia (massless dummy)
            mass = 1e-6
            inertia = np.array([1e-9, 1e-9, 1e-9], dtype=np.float32)  # Diagonal inertia
            dummy_link.set_mass_and_inertia(mass, sapien.Pose(), inertia)
            # No visual for dummy links (not needed)

            # Set joint properties
            dummy_link.set_joint_name(f"ycb_joint_{joint_name}")
            dummy_link.set_joint_properties(
                type=joint_type,
                limits=[limits],
                pose_in_parent=sapien.Pose(),
                pose_in_child=sapien.Pose(),
                friction=0.0,
                damping=10.0,  # Initially free
            )

            self._ycb_joint_names.append(f"ycb_joint_{joint_name}")
            current_parent = dummy_link

        # Create final YCB link with actual geometry
        ycb_link = builder.create_link_builder(current_parent)
        ycb_link.set_name("ycb_object_link")

        # Add YCB object geometry (bowl as example)
        self._add_ycb_geometry_to_link(ycb_link)

        # Final revolute joint
        joint_name, joint_type, _, limits = joint_configs[-1]
        ycb_link.set_joint_name(f"ycb_joint_{joint_name}")
        ycb_link.set_joint_properties(
            type=joint_type,
            limits=[limits],
            pose_in_parent=sapien.Pose(),
            pose_in_child=sapien.Pose(),
            friction=0.0,
            damping=10.0,
        )
        self._ycb_joint_names.append(f"ycb_joint_{joint_name}")
```

    def _after_init(self) -> None:
        """After initialization, cache YCB joint and link references."""
        super()._after_init()

        # Cache YCB joints
        self.ycb_joints = []
        for joint_name in self._ycb_joint_names:
            for joint in self.robot.get_joints():
                if joint.name.endswith(joint_name):
                    self.ycb_joints.append(joint)
                    break

        # Cache YCB link
        for link in self.robot.get_links():
            if link.name.endswith("ycb_object_link"):
                self.ycb_link = link
                break

        # Disable collision between YCB object and fingers
        # Set the same collision group bit for YCB link and finger links
        if self.ycb_link is not None:
            self.ycb_link.set_collision_group_bit(
                group=2, bit_idx=YCB_FINGER_COLLISION_BIT, bit=1
            )
            # Also set for both finger links
            self.finger1_link.set_collision_group_bit(
                group=2, bit_idx=YCB_FINGER_COLLISION_BIT, bit=1
            )
            self.finger2_link.set_collision_group_bit(
                group=2, bit_idx=YCB_FINGER_COLLISION_BIT, bit=1
            )

            # Enable gravity so object can fall when unlocked
            # We use very low mass (1g) so PD controller can easily hold it when locked
            self.ycb_link.disable_gravity = False

        # Initialize YCB joints to locked state (high stiffness/damping)
        for joint in self.ycb_joints:
            joint.set_drive_properties(
                stiffness=1e6, damping=1e6, force_limit=1e6
            )

    def lock_ycb_to_hand(self, env_idx: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None):
        """Lock YCB object to hand by setting high stiffness/damping.

        Args:
            env_idx: Optional indices of environments to lock. If None, locks all.
        """
        if len(self.ycb_joints) == 0:
            return


        # Set very high stiffness and damping to lock joints
        # Use acceleration mode for better control
        for joint in self.ycb_joints:
            # Set extremely high stiffness/damping to create rigid attachment
            # Use acceleration mode which is more direct than force mode
            # Drive target is implicitly zero (from initialization)
            for obj in joint._objs:
                obj.set_drive_properties(
                    stiffness=1e8, damping=1e7, force_limit=1e10
                )
                # Also set high friction to passively resist movement
                obj.set_friction(1e6)

        if env_idx is None:
            self._ycb_is_grasped[:] = True
        else:
            self._ycb_is_grasped[env_idx] = True
```

    def unlock_ycb_from_hand(self, env_idx: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None):
        """Unlock YCB object by setting zero stiffness/damping.

        Args:
            env_idx: Optional indices of environments to unlock. If None, unlocks all.
        """
        if len(self.ycb_joints) == 0:
            return


        # Set zero stiffness and damping to make joints free
        for joint in self.ycb_joints:
            for obj in joint._objs:
                obj.set_drive_properties(
                    stiffness=0.0, damping=0.0, force_limit=0.0
                )
                # Also set high friction to passively resist movement
                obj.set_friction(0.0)

        if env_idx is None:
            self._ycb_is_grasped[:] = False
        else:
            self._ycb_is_grasped[env_idx] = False

I am facing an issue where the robotic arm in the simulator cannot pick up objects. The arm successfully moves to the target grasp position, closes the gripper, but the object remains stationary and is not lifted.
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/159beff9-dd53-4e5b-ab5a-6d46b2e56d0e

The agent class is:

class A1Arm(BaseAgent):

        _materials=dict(

        ),

            gripper1_axis=dict(

            ),
        ),
    )

    fix_root_link = True

    keyframes = dict()

    gripper_joint_names = [
        "gripper1_axis", 
        "gripper2_axis"
    ]
    ee_link_name = "arm_seg6"

    arm_stiffness = 1e3
    arm_damping = 2e2
    arm_force_limit = 100.0

    gripper_stiffness = 1e3
    gripper_damping = 2e2
    gripper_force_limit = 100.0

    @property
    def _controller_configs(self):
        # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
        # Arm
        # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
        arm_pd_joint_pos = PDJointPosControllerConfig(
            self.arm_joint_names,
            lower=None,
            upper=None,
            stiffness=self.arm_stiffness,
            damping=self.arm_damping,
            force_limit=self.arm_force_limit,
            normalize_action=False,
        )
        arm_pd_joint_pos_vel = PDJointPosVelControllerConfig(
            self.arm_joint_names,
            lower=-0.1,
            upper=0.1,
            stiffness=self.arm_stiffness,
            damping=self.arm_damping,
            force_limit=self.arm_force_limit,
            normalize_action=False,
        )
        # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
        # Gripper
        # -------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
        # NOTE(jigu): IssacGym uses large P and D but with force limit
        # However, tune a good force limit to have a good mimic behavior
        gripper_pd_joint_pos = PDJointPosMimicControllerConfig(
            self.gripper_joint_names,
            lower=None,  # a trick to have force when the object is thin
            upper=None,
            stiffness=self.gripper_stiffness,
            damping=self.gripper_damping,
            force_limit=self.gripper_force_limit,
            normalize_action=False,
        )

            pd_joint_pos=dict(arm=arm_pd_joint_pos, gripper=gripper_pd_joint_pos),
            pd_joint_pos_vel=dict(arm=arm_pd_joint_pos_vel, gripper=gripper_pd_joint_pos),

        self.gripper_joint_indices = get_active_joint_indices(self.robot, self.gripper_joint_names)

        self.ee_link = sapien_utils.get_obj_by_name(
            self.robot.get_links(), self.ee_link_name
        )
    
    def is_grasping(self, object: Actor, min_force: float = 0.5, max_angle: float = 85):
        """Check if the robot is grasping an object

        Args:
            object (Actor): The object to check if the robot is grasping
            min_force (float, optional): Minimum force before the robot is considered to be grasping the object in Newtons. Defaults to 0.5.
            max_angle (int, optional): Maximum angle of contact to consider grasping. Defaults to 85.
        """
        l_contact_forces = self.scene.get_pairwise_contact_forces(
            self.gripper1_link, object
        )
        r_contact_forces = self.scene.get_pairwise_contact_forces(
            self.gripper2_link, object
        )
        lforce = torch.linalg.norm(l_contact_forces, axis=1)
        rforce = torch.linalg.norm(r_contact_forces, axis=1)

        # direction to open the gripper
        ldirection = self.gripper1_link.pose.to_transformation_matrix()[..., :3, 1]
        rdirection = -self.gripper2_link.pose.to_transformation_matrix()[..., :3, 1]
        langle = common.compute_angle_between(ldirection, l_contact_forces)
        rangle = common.compute_angle_between(rdirection, r_contact_forces)
        lflag = torch.logical_and(
            lforce >= min_force, torch.rad2deg(langle) <= max_angle
        )
        rflag = torch.logical_and(
            rforce >= min_force, torch.rad2deg(rangle) <= max_angle
        )
        return torch.logical_and(lflag, rflag)

body:
Hi!

I created a custom task on top of PickCube that loads a 3D scene from the Matterport3D dataset to add visual distractions during model evaluation. The function to load the scene looks like this:

```
def load_Matterport(builder):
    paths = sorted(list(glob.glob(os.path.join("./data/matterport3d/*.glb"))))
    path = random.choice(paths)
    pose = Pose(q=[0, 0, 0, 1])  # y-axis up for Matterport scenes
    # Add offset to workspace
    offset = np.array([0, 0, 0.8])
    builder.initial_pose = Pose(-offset)
    builder.add_visual_from_file(path, pose)
    actor = builder.build_static(name='background')
    # actor.set_pose(Pose(-offset))
    return actor
```

and is called inside a custom subclass of `TableSceneBuilder` like this:

```
class RandomBackgroundTableSceneBuilder(TableSceneBuilder):
    def build(self):
      ...
      load_Matterport(builder)
      builder.add_visual_from_file(
          filename=table_model_file, scale=[scale] * 3, pose=table_pose
      )
      ...
```

which then gets used inside the `_load_scene` function. 

However, I run into the following error when I try to render a rollout from this env with `render_mode=human`:

`RuntimeError: Modifying a scene (add/remove object/camera) is not allowed after creating the batched render system.`

This is easily avoidable by setting the sim_backed to CPU, however if I train the model with sim_backend=gpu (which I am to leverage parallel env training), then evaluating the model with sim_backend=cpu results in significantly worse performance. Not sure if this is a known consequence of using different rendering backends or a bug, but just thought I'd bring it up here in case it's a solvable problem. 

Thanks!

I think there may be some issue at the moment with using the viewer in addition to running GPU parallelized rendering. Someone raised the same issue on discord (which I am not sure how to link to on github). I'll try and get around to investigating this, this issue has been around for months now. 

A temporary workaround is to train on the GPU backend, evaluate on the GPU backend and save trajectories with the `RecordEpisode` wrapper. Now if you want to use the viewer (done with render_mode=human), you can replay collected trajectories on the GPU in the CPU environment using environment states by doing a for loop like

```
state_dicts = load_state_dicts_from_trajectory.h5
env = gym.make(env_id, num_envs=1, render_mode="human", **other_env_kwargs)
for i in range(100):
  env.set_state_dict(state_dicts[i])
  env.render_human() # or env.render() if render_mode=="human"
```

This is in fact how all of the nice videos/photos are generated usually on our documentation since high quality ray-tracing only works with the single CPU sim at the moment. body:
Hello, I have encountered this issue: pixels shift occur in the vector environment when the camera configurations are modified with a smaller image width.

```python
from mani_skill2.vector import make
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

venv = make('LiftCube-v0', 1, obs_mode='rgbd', reward_mode='sparse', camera_cfgs={'base_camera': {'width': 97}})
obs = venv.reset()
venv.close()

plt.imshow(obs['image']['base_camera']['rgb'].cpu().numpy()[0])
```
![image](https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill2/assets/62796258/85aa7640-3979-4525-8146-66a4632574e6)

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
Thanks for bringing it up, we will take a look.

Curious though why did you try width of 97?

comments.author: Yefanov
comments.body: I just picked a random prime number. Initially, I worked with ms1 environments and modified the camera configurations from robot-based 160x400 to static 128x128. I chose a prime number because using 128x64 would result in a squeezed image. I wanted to avoid any common divisors that could lead to incorrect assumptions.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body: Looks like you are quite spot on. We aren't sure just yet what the bug is but a temporary solution is to ensure the camera sizes for both hand and base cameras are the same. That seems to fix the bug.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
Actually we know what the bug is. The bug is at the ManiSkill2 level. What happens is the vec env observations are padded because one camera is smaller. That's where the black part comes in. The RGBDVecEnv wrapper does not handle the padding quite correctly.

If you reallly want to use a prime number width, check the VecEnv wrapper and `_get_torch_observations` function, and instead of doing `tensor = tensor[:, :h, :w]` at line 257, first flatten the tensor, take the first w * h * 4 elements (padding goes on the end), then reshape to (w, h, 4). Otherwise just use same camera sizes.

comments.author: Yefanov
comments.body:
This "fix" works for me (line 247 of vec_env.py):

```python
tensor = tensor[:, :w].flatten().reshape((-1, h, w, 4))
```

However, this will fail when used with an image height smaller than the default.

The issue is that padding always gets added to the bottom of an image. But when using a smaller width, padding should be added to the right side of the image.

In any case, using the same camera sizes is the solution for me. Thank you!

factor_evidence_quote: the RGBDVecEnv wrapper does not handle the padding quite correctly.
phase_evidence_quote: the RGBDVecEnv wrapper does not handle the padding quite correctly.
title: Pixels shift occur in the vector environment when using smaller image width for camera

When running the baseline.sh script for ACT, a Key error raises when evaluating the environment.

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/lzanetti/workspaces/latent_vla_ws/src/ManiSkill/examples/baselines/act/train.py", line 428, in <module>
    eval_metrics = evaluate(args.num_eval_episodes, ema_agent, envs, eval_kwargs)
                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/lzanetti/workspaces/latent_vla_ws/src/ManiSkill/examples/baselines/act/act/evaluate.py", line 83, in evaluate
    if isinstance(info["final_info"], dict):
                  ~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'final_info'

This is because when running train.py, using "physx_cpu", the CPUGymWrapper is used and that does not include "final_info" in the info dict when truncation/termination happens

comments.author: luokuang2001
comments.body:
I encountered the same issue as well.
Could you please let me know the recommended way to resolve this?

comments.author: JXZhou0224
comments.body:
I have a solution for this. In ManiSkill/baselines/act/act/evaluate.py:
https://github.com/mani-skill/ManiSkill/blob/b860fb7fc8ce086fb5f27f554f9c7146650f1cee/examples/baselines/act/act/evaluate.py#L79-L89

Add a case to detect cpu simulated environments. 
```python
...
if truncated.any():
    assert truncated.all() == truncated.any(), "all episodes should truncate at the same time for fair evaluation with other algorithms"
    if sim_backend == "physx_cpu":
        for k, v in info["episode"].items():
            eval_metrics[k].append(v)
    elif isinstance(info["final_info"], dict):
...
```

In gpu envs, if the environment auto resets when a subscene is finished, the eval_metric infos are overwritten to the reset state, so we need "final_info" to store whether the last simulation succeeded.
https://github.com/mani-skill/ManiSkill/blob/b860fb7fc8ce086fb5f27f554f9c7146650f1cee/mani_skill/vector/wrappers/gymnasium.py#L164-L177

In this case, since cpu env doesn't do auto resets, the info at the final timestep is the actual task eval results, so we don't need a "final_info" field to store it.

This is a bug that probably appears in all the `evaluate.py` across all the baseline implementations, and the same fix can be adapted to all of them

**Description**: I am encountering a severe inconsistency between the CPU and GPU simulation backends. The same planner/policy performs significantly worse or fails completely when running on the GPU backend compared to the CPU backend. This issue manifests in two different scenarios:

**Scenario 1: Motion Planning with Official Tasks**

I tested the official motion planner across multiple tasks using the GPU backend. I observed a pattern where some tasks consistently fail on GPU, while others work fine (CPU simulation works well for all tasks).

- GPU simulation fails in: `StackCube-v1`, `PegInsertionSide-v1`, `PlaceSphere-v1`, `LiftPegUpright-v1`, etc.
- GPU simulation succeeds in: `PickCube-v1`, `PushCube-v1`, `PullCube-v1`, `StackPyramid-v1`, etc.

For example,  for `StackCube-v1`, GPU-simulated motion planning consistently fails. It appears that the target grasp position is calculated or retrieved incorrectly in the GPU environment, leading to planning failures.

Reproduction Command:

```bash
# CPU simulation
python mani_skill/examples/motionplanning/panda/run.py -e "StackCube-v1" -r "panda" --traj-name "panda_test" -n 1 --sim-backend "physx_cpu" --only-count-success --save-video
# GPU simulation
python mani_skill/examples/motionplanning/panda/run.py -e "StackCube-v1" -r "panda" --traj-name "panda_test" -n 1 --sim-backend "physx_cuda" --only-count-success --save-video --render-mode "human"

body:
Hi,

Before asking my question, I would like to thank you for providing a great benchmark.

My issue is that the baseline code for Diffusion Policy does not achieve the expected performance in the PushT-v1 environment. I would appreciate any suggestions for improvement.

To verify whether the baseline code works as intended, I ran the shell script [baseline.sh](https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/blob/5fb50fdeca88f23f8315cc32200d3d67247802b8/examples/baselines/diffusion_policy/baselines.sh) while disabling other environments.

Before running this script, I downloaded the [demonstration data](https://maniskill.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/learning_from_demos/setup.html) and executed [this script](https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/blob/5fb50fdeca88f23f8315cc32200d3d67247802b8/scripts/data_generation/replay_for_il_baselines.sh#L32) to generate state-based demonstration data.

The trained model exhibits poor success rates, ranging between 0.15 and 0.2, as shown in the image below.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b7152e41-a799-422c-89af-fd332c0a7506)

However, according to the paper ["Responsive Noise-Relaying Diffusion Policy: Responsive and Efficient Visuomotor Control"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12724) (page 8), the state-based diffusion policy in the PushT-v1 environment should achieve a success rate between 0.4 and 0.5.

I have carefully reviewed the parameters and detailed settings, and they appear to be identical in both the paper and this repository.

Since one of the contributors is an author of the paper, I assume there might be additional details required to reproduce the exact results.

Does this script produce the same results as reported in the paper? What would be the best approach to accurately reproduce the results?

Thank you.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body: @xiuyuan0216 is the author on the paper and knows the details better. I think he uses either a slightly different DP or may have made some other changes compared to the default one on maniskill.

comments.author: xiuyuan0216
comments.body:
@SieRaX 

Thank you for your interest in the ManiSkill3 benchmark and for taking the time to read our newly released paper!

Although we used our own implementation of Diffusion Policy (DP) instead of the one provided by ManiSkill3, I can still reproduce the performance reported in our paper using the ManiSkill3 DP code.

One key detail to pay attention to is the number of demonstrations used for training. If you run the provided script directly, it sets demos=100 by default, meaning only 100 demonstrations are used for DP training. However, the full dataset actually contains around 700 demonstrations. By training on the entire dataset, I can achieve over 40% success rate using the ManiSkill3 DP code.

Please feel free to reach out to me at x1yuan@ucsd.edu if you have any further questions!

body:
Hi ManiSkill team, thanks for the great benchmark and simulator.

I am trying to reproduce the PushT-v1 task (ManiSkill3) using offline imitation learning (Diffusion Policy–style training). However, I am encountering very low evaluation success rates , and after further investigation I suspect there may be an issue with the provided RL demonstration dataset.

Below are the details.

1.Observed Problem Extremely low evaluation success rate, as demonstrated on official WandB results provided for PushT-v1。
2. Replay of RL demonstrations performs poorly
To diagnose the issue, I replayed the RL trajectories directly using the official replay script:
```
python -m mani_skill.trajectory.replay_trajectory \
  --traj-path ~/.maniskill/demos/PushT-v1/rl/xxxx \
  --vis
```
I see most replayed trajectories fail to complete the task.The pusher often:
Misses the target region, repeat a single motion again and again, terminates far from success.

Overall behavior looks suboptimal and unstable, even though these are supposed to be RL-generated demonstrations
This happens consistently across multiple trajectories I tested.

Why this is concerning:
Offline imitation learning performance is upper-bounded by demonstration quality
If the RL demonstrations themselves fail when replayed.This makes it difficult to reproduce PushT-v1 baselines.

Questions / Clarification Requests:
1.Are the provided PushT-v1 RL demonstrations expected to succeed when replayed?
2.Which policy / checkpoint were these RL demonstrations generated from?
3.Is there a known issue with the PushT-v1 RL dataset in ManiSkill3?

class Hobot2BridgeFlatTable(WidowX250SBridgeDatasetFlatTable):

        height = 128 * scale
        intrinsic = np.array([[124.409, 0, 114.0], [0, 124.409, 64.0],

                    [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0],

                entity_uid="base_link",
                width=width,
                height=height,
                near=0.01,
                far=2.0,
                intrinsic=intrinsic,
            ),
        ]

    @property
    def _controller_configs(self):
        arm_common_kwargs = dict(
            joint_names=self.arm_joint_names,
            lower=None,
            upper=None,
            stiffness=np.array(self.arm_stiffness) * 2.0,
            damping=self.arm_damping,
            force_limit=self.arm_force_limit,
            friction=self.arm_friction,
            use_delta=False,
            interpolate=True,
            normalize_action=False,
        )
        arm_pd_absolute_joint_target = PDJointPosControllerConfig(
            **arm_common_kwargs)

        gripper_pd_joint_pos = PDJointPosMimicControllerConfig(
            joint_names=self.gripper_joint_names,
            lower=-0.04,
            upper=0.04,
            stiffness=self.gripper_stiffness,
            damping=self.gripper_damping,
            force_limit=self.gripper_force_limit,
            normalize_action=True,
            drive_mode="force",
        )
        controller = dict(arm=arm_pd_absolute_joint_target,
                          gripper=gripper_pd_joint_pos)
        return dict(
            arm_pd_absolute_joint_target_gripper_pd_joint_pos=controller)

body:
## Missing VecEnv Wrapper
For submission, you provided the ```run_evaluation.py``` and ```evaluator.py``` scripts in the **ManiSkill2** repository (```/mani_skill2/evaluation/```).

In the ```Evaluation``` class in your **ManiSkill2-Learn** repository (```maniskill2_learn/env/evaluation.py```), you correctly wrap the raw OpenAI gym environment with your MS2-specific wrappers *(UnifiedVectorEnvAPI<VectorEnvBase<BufferAugmentedEnv<ExtendedEnv<TimeLimit<ManiSkill2_ObsWrapper<RenderInfoWrapper<...>>>>>>)*.

But in the ```evaluator.py``` script, you do not wrap the raw Gymnasium environment with these wrappers. 
```
self.env: BaseEnv = gym.make(
    self.env_id,
    obs_mode=obs_mode,
    control_mode=control_mode,
    render_mode=render_mode,
    **self.env_kwargs
)
self.policy = policy_cls(
    self.env_id, self.env.observation_space, self.env.action_space
)
self.result = OrderedDict()
```
This is problematic because our trained models rely on the frame transformations, normalizations, downsampling, and shape adjustments of the observations.

Therefore, we added these wrappers in our code, but this is definitely not desirable.

## Inconsistent observation shapes
Furthermore, the values in `self.env.observation_space` are inconsistent with those provided by `get_env_info()` in the `maniskill2_learn.env` folder. 

To obtain the size of the `state` vector, we summed up the sizes of all corresponding vectors in `self.env.observation_space` in the following fashion.
```
state_shape = 0
agent_space = observation_space['agent']
extra_space = observation_space['extra']
for space in [agent_space, extra_space]:
    for key in space.keys():
        if len(space[key].shape) == 0:
            state_shape += 1
        else:
            state_shape += space[key].shape[0]
```
However, the final value in `state_shape` exceeds the true value provided by `get_env_info()` by 8 in case of the `StackCube-v0` and `TurnFaucet-v0` environments.
Of course, we replaced the env_name in our environment config `env_cfg` by the value in `env_id`.
```
env_cfg.env_name = env_id
env_params = get_env_info(env_cfg)
obs_shape = env_params["obs_shape"]
action_shape = env_params["action_shape"]
```
For the `StackCube-v0` environment, we have `state_shape`=32, while the value in `env_params` is 24.
For the `TurnFaucet-v0` environment, we similarly have `state_shape`=39, while the value in `env_params` is 31.

The latter way of computing the observation shapes with `get_env_info()` is also used in your aforementioned `Evaluation` class and is hence consistent with the values received during training. 
In our `user_solution.py`, we thus ignored the `observation_spaces` parameter and instead fetched the space specifications from `get_env_info()`.

But we think this might possibly be an error in your example script.

comments.author: Vector215
comments.body:
After comparative experiments and code review, I've roughly confirmed why the success rates of pick cube and push cube differ so drastically.

Because in the original baseline for pick cube, even when trained using RGB, state elements were added. You can see that the `Goal_site` object is a `_hidden_object`, so it doesn't appear in the RGB's `obs`, but its position is passed to the state via extra `obs`. This results in the state of this task having 29 dimensions, while other tasks have 25 dimensions (four more dimensions: `is_grasped` and `goal_pos`).

Therefore, the original baseline pick cube task had a difficulty level similar to half state + half RGB, which I think is reasonable because there's a progression in task difficulty.

I tried removing `goal_site` from the `hidden_object` list and removing the extra `is_grasped` and `goal_pos` effects on the state in the wrapper. This task quickly became much harder, similar to the stack cube case, with a success rate approaching 0.

I would greatly appreciate it if you could verify and discuss this.

This suggests that the low RGB-based success rate may be partly due to weak visual representation rather than only a diffusion policy implementation issue. Since StackCube requires precise object localization and relative spatial reasoning, improving the visual encoder seems to make a clear difference.

body:
Hi,  
When training RL agents on Push Cube, I noticed that sometimes, the agent can get stuck in a local minima where it will pick up the cube and hold it up above the target.  

**SAC State**   

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8e62a30c-f508-4382-8f60-9f11883c3036
   
**DrQ-V2 (RGB)**  

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b66c0883-7306-4074-b993-47e53c0516aa

  

When `success == True` the reward is set to the maximum value of 3 :  
```python
reward[info["success"]] = 3
```  
And the [success computation](https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/blob/ba3562f5a6cfda7b7a534aac7aeb233d2c3cb362/mani_skill/envs/tasks/tabletop/push_cube.py#L183-L188) depends on the z-axis (good) :  
```
# success is achieved when the cube's xy position on the table is within the
# goal region's area (a circle centered at the goal region's xy position) and
# the cube is still on the surface
is_obj_placed = (
    torch.linalg.norm(
        self.obj.pose.p[..., :2] - self.goal_region.pose.p[..., :2], axis=1
    )
    < self.goal_radius
) & (self.obj.pose.p[..., 2] < self.cube_half_size + 5e-3)

return {
    "success": is_obj_placed,
}
```
But when `success == False` , the reward has the [following component](https://github.com/haosulab/ManiSkill/blob/ba3562f5a6cfda7b7a534aac7aeb233d2c3cb362/mani_skill/envs/tasks/tabletop/push_cube.py#L224-L227) :  
```python
obj_to_goal_dist = torch.linalg.norm(
    self.obj.pose.p[..., :2] - self.goal_region.pose.p[..., :2], axis=1
)
place_reward = 1 - torch.tanh(5 * obj_to_goal_dist)
reward += place_reward * reached
```  
Therefore the reward does not seem to use the z axis when `success == False` which could encourage the sub-optimal  behavior mentioned.  
   
# Suggestion
My suggestion would be to add the z axis to the reward for the case where `success == False` so that the agent is still incentivized to keep the cube on the table.

comments.author: StoneT2000
comments.body:
If it holds it up above the target as long as success is true it doesn't matter?

Only concern would be if the success condition permits the cube to too high above the target (not really pushing it forward anymore)

comments.author: AlexandreBrown
comments.body:
@StoneT2000 Even when receiving non-zero success rate during training, the current reward formulation can lead to sub-optimal behavior where the policy games the system by holding the cube above the target on purpose.  
It might not look like it but **the success rate was 0% for the Drq-V2 (eval) video example** I posted, this means that all rollouts have the robot bring the cube above the target. This is the video we get after training for 1M steps and during training we get non-zero success rate quite often I would say.  
I also see a trend in the eval success rate, initially the policies tend to learn the optimal behavior but then as training continues it discovers how to cheat the reward.
   
Perhaps testing a reward that includes z would be worth the try.

comments.body:
Sure. It is still strange it is unable to solve it as it learns to grasp the cube even when pushing it is faster.

Let me know how your reward tuning goes.

comments.author: xuanlinli17
comments.body:
Actually the dataset is converted to part of the "Open-X-embodiment" dataset. The action is unbounded. Action [:3] is xyz movement of tool-center point (tcp, or center between two Panda gripper fingers), action [3:6] is axis-angle movement of tcp, axis[6:7] is gripper open/close.   0.1 times xyz value maps to meters, and 0.1 times axis-angle maps to rotation at the same axis but norm in radians (due to the controller configuration below)

For meaning of action[:6], it actually corresponds to a controller config not yet included in the original ManiSkill2 implementation (`agents/configs/panda/defaults.py`), for the "base-frame conformity" with other Open-X-Embodiment datasets:

```
arm_pd_base_ee_delta_pose = PDEEPoseControllerConfig(
            self.arm_joint_names,
            -0.1,
            0.1,
            0.1,
            self.arm_stiffness,
            self.arm_damping,
            self.arm_force_limit,
            ee_link=self.ee_link_name,
            frame="base",
        )
 ```
 
 Which means the action[:6] is the "target delta pose" of tcp with respect to the base frame of the robot. A caveat is that for ManiSkill2, the tcp target pose after applying the action is `sapien.core.Pose(p=scale * action[:3], q=quaternion_multiplication(axangle2quat(scale * action[3:6]), robot_tcp_pose_wrt_base))` (where `scale=0.1`, `robot_tcp_pose_wrt_base = robot.pose.inv() * robot.tcp.pose`, and `quaternion_multiplication(a, b) = sapien.core.Pose(q=a) * sapien.core.Pose(q=b)`),   while for other subsets of Open-X-Embodiment datasets it is mostly `sapien.core.Pose(p=robot_tcp_pose_wrt_base.p + (potentially scaled) action[:3], q=quaternion_multiplication(euler2quat(*(potentially scaled action[3:6])), robot_tcp_pose_wrt_base.q))`. This means that in the current tfds maniskill dataset, we don't decouple translation and rotation actions when calculating the new tcp pose, while for other parts of the open-x-embodiment dataset they decouple it.

comments.body:
This is a **protocol version mismatch** between your local install and the Docker image.

The `libero:latest` Docker image includes the newer HELLO handshake protocol, but your locally installed `vla-eval` doesn't recognize the `hello` message type — which is exactly what the smoke test error shows:

```
ValueError: Unknown message type: 'hello'. Valid types: ['observation', 'action', 'episode_start', 'episode_end', 'error']
```

**Fix**: Update your local code to the latest version:

```bash
git pull origin main
uv sync --python 3.11 --all-extras --dev
```

This will bring your local model server in sync with the Docker image's protocol.
